cocktails.name: Irish Coffee
cocktails.method: Add whisky, water and syrup to irish coffee glass. Pour a fresh single espresso on top. Layer with chantilly, garnish with grated nutmeg
cocktails.garnish: Grated Nutmeg
cocktails.tasting_notes: Breakfast and nightcap in one glass. Fresh espresso and stout syrup bring dark, roasty, malty bitterness, with soft Irish whiskey warming it through. Cold chantilly cream floats on top, so every sip goes hot through cold. Finishes long with coffee, toasted malt and a whisper of nutmeg.
cocktails.history: Born in 1943 at the Foynes flying-boat terminal near Limerick, when chef Joe Sheridan had to thaw out a planeload of Pan Am passengers turned back by bad weather. Someone asked if it was Brazilian coffee. 'No,' he said, 'that's Irish coffee.' In 1952 travel writer Stanton Delaplane drank one at Shannon Airport and took the idea to the Buena Vista Café in San Francisco, which still pours them by the thousand. Sheridan ended up moving out there to work for them. Our twist: stout syrup instead of sugar, and fresh espresso.

cocktails.name: Nassau Boulevard
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients in mixing glass with ice, strain into a rocks glass with a large cube, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange peel, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: A Boulevardier on holiday. Campari and sweet vermouth bring the bittersweet backbone, bourbon adds caramel and oak, and the Planteray rums sneak in molasses, pineapple and a lick of coconut. Dark and moody, with sunshine underneath. Finishes long and warm with orange peel and dark sugar.
cocktails.history: Our own riff on the Boulevardier, named for Charles's childhood in Nassau, Bahamas. The Campari and sweet vermouth stay, but the bourbon has to share: Evan Williams sits alongside Planteray Stiggins' Fancy pineapple rum and Cut & Dry coconut rum, giving a Paris classic a Caribbean passport. The original Boulevardier was first printed in Harry MacElhone's Barflies and Cocktails (Paris, 1927), credited to Erskine Gwynne, an American expat who ran a Paris magazine called Boulevardier.

cocktails.name: Jungle Bird
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients, fill your glass with 3/4 crushed ice, single strain, top with a little crushed ice mount. Garnish
cocktails.garnish: Maraschino Cherry, Lime Wedge
cocktails.tasting_notes: Tiki with a bitter streak. Juicy pineapple crashes into Campari's bitter orange, while dark rum and Appleton 8 bring molasses, oak and proper Jamaican funk. Lime keeps the whole thing awake. Finishes dry and bitter, with pineapple hanging around.
cocktails.history: Created by beverage manager Jeffrey Ong as the welcome drink for the Kuala Lumpur Hilton, which opened on 6 July 1973. It was named after the tropical birds in the aviary visible from the hotel's Aviary Bar, and was first served in a ceramic bird-shaped vessel. Its first appearance in print, John J. Poister's New American Bartender's Guide (1989), dated it 1978, which is why you'll still see that year quoted. Jeff 'Beachbum' Berry revived it in Intoxica! (2002). Malaysia's only internationally recognised classic, and an IBA official cocktail since 2024.

cocktails.name: Boulevardier
cocktails.method: Stir all in mixing glass, strain in rocks glass with a large cube, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange peel, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: The Negroni's American cousin. Bourbon steps in for gin, bringing caramel and vanilla to Campari's bitter orange and the vermouth's herbal sweetness. Rounder, deeper and a touch more dangerous than a Negroni. Finishes long with orange peel, dark cherry and oak.
cocktails.history: First printed in Harry MacElhone's Barflies and Cocktails (Paris, 1927), where writer Arthur Moss credits it to Erskine Gwynne, a young American socialite who ran a Paris expat magazine called Boulevardier (1927–32). So yes, it's named after a magazine. The original was equal parts Campari, Italian vermouth and bourbon. Forgotten for decades, it came roaring back in the 2000s cocktail revival and is now an IBA official cocktail.

cocktails.name: A Rabbit's Foot
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with ice, Double Strain into a chilled rocks glass, ice and garnish.
cocktails.garnish: Lime Wedge, Mint Sprig, Angostura Spray
cocktails.tasting_notes: Orchard meets tiki. Calvados brings baked apple, rum adds body and a splash of agricole gives grassy funk. Pineapple liqueur, orgeat and lime build a Mai Tai-style core underneath. Finishes long and nutty, with almond, apple and a flicker of Peychaud's anise.
cocktails.history: Starts life as the Rabbit's Foot in Stanley M. Jones' Jones' Complete Barguide (1977): apple brandy and rum shaken with orange juice, lemon juice and grenadine. A decent drink, but we've sent it to the tropics. Busnel VSOP calvados, Planteray 3 Stars and Saint James agricole blanc make the base, with pineapple liqueur and orgeat in place of the juices and grenadine, turning it into a Mai Tai-style riff. The name also nods to Charles's film magazine, A Rabbit's Foot.

cocktails.name: Espresso Martini
cocktails.method: Shake hard all ingredients with ice, double strain in a chilled coupe. Garnish
cocktails.garnish: Line of Choco Powder
cocktails.tasting_notes: The drink that keeps the night going. Fresh espresso brings roasted bitterness, coffee liqueur adds sweetness and depth, and clean vodka keeps it sharp. Shaken hard for that thick, velvety crema. Finishes dry with dark coffee and a hint of cocoa.
cocktails.history: Created by Dick Bradsell around 1983 at the Soho Brasserie on Old Compton Street, London, when a model asked for something to 'wake me up, then f*** me up'. The espresso machine happened to sit right next to his station. It started on the rocks as the Vodka Espresso, became the Pharmaceutical Stimulant at Pharmacy in Notting Hill, and was finally reworked as the Espresso Martini at Match EC1 in 1997. Guests will tell you the model was Kate Moss or Naomi Campbell. In 1983 they were about 9 and 13, so no.
cocktails.notes: Aim for a fluffy and decadent foam.

cocktails.name: Aperol Spritz
cocktails.method: Build in wine glass, aperol first, ice, garnish, straw, and top up with Franciacorta
cocktails.garnish: 1x Orange Wedge
cocktails.tasting_notes: Sunshine in a glass. Aperol's orange, rhubarb and gentle bitterness meet crisp, toasty Franciacorta. Light, fizzy and low in alcohol, so a second one is always on the cards. Finishes dry and refreshing with zesty orange.
cocktails.history: The spritz goes back to the 19th-century Veneto, then ruled by the Austrian Empire, where Habsburg soldiers found the local wine too strong and asked for a 'spritz' (German for splash) of water. Aperol came later, launched by brothers Luigi and Silvio Barbieri of Padua at the 1919 Padua Trade Fair. Mixing it with sparkling wine and soda caught on in the 1950s. Then Campari Group bought the brand in 2003, pushed the 3-2-1 serve hard, and the rest is every beer garden in Europe.
cocktails.notes: Sulphites Allergens

cocktails.name: Bee's Knees
cocktails.method: Shake all with ice, double strain in chilled coupe. Garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon peel, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: Sunny, floral and dangerously smooth. Fresh lemon and honey give a rounded sweet-sour balance, with London Dry juniper underneath and orange bitters adding lift. Finishes clean with honey and citrus peel.
cocktails.history: A gin sour sweetened with honey, named after 1920s slang for 'the best'. The first printed recipe is in Cocktails de Paris (1929), credited to Frank Meier of the Ritz Paris. The same year, a Brooklyn newspaper credited it to Margaret 'Molly' Brown, the Titanic survivor who spent much of her time in Paris, so Meier may well have made it for her. You'll often hear it was invented to hide the taste of bathtub gin. Nice story, zero evidence.
cocktails.notes: Honeysuckle - Swap the gin with Planteray 3* -------------------------------- Honey Bee - Swap the gin with Appleton 8y

cocktails.name: Daiquiri
cocktails.method: Shake all with ice, Double Strain in chilled coupe.
cocktails.garnish: None
cocktails.tasting_notes: Three ingredients and nowhere to hide. Funky, characterful white rum, fresh lime and just enough sugar. Bright, tart and bone-dry when it's made right. Finishes clean with lime zest and a lingering rum note.
cocktails.history: Named after the beach and iron mines of Daiquirí near Santiago de Cuba. People had been mixing rum, lime and sugar in the Caribbean for centuries, but the name is credited to American mining engineer Jennings Cox around 1900, and his handwritten recipe sits in the University of Miami archives. In 1909 US Navy medical officer Lucius W. Johnson took it home to the Army and Navy Club in Washington, D.C. Then in the 1920s and 30s, Constantino Ribalaigua Vert at El Floridita in Havana made it world-famous, with a little help from regular Ernest Hemingway.
cocktails.notes: The balance of citrus and sweetner, the corect dilution and aeration from the shaking, and the complexity of the rum are all key to make this drink perfeclty.

cocktails.name: Sidecar
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with ice, Double Strain in sugar-rimmed chilled coupe
cocktails.garnish: Half Sugar Rim, Lemon Peel, express over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: Classy, tart and grown-up. Cognac's dried fruit and oak meet dry curaçao's bitter orange and sharp lemon, while Pineau des Charentes adds juicy grape roundness. The half sugar rim lets each guest choose how sweet each sip is. Finishes long with orange peel and warm brandy.
cocktails.history: First printed in 1922 in two books at once: Harry MacElhone's ABC of Mixing Cocktails and Robert Vermeire's Cocktails: How to Mix Them. Vermeire credited it to Pat MacGarry of Buck's Club, London. MacElhone later claimed it for Harry's New York Bar in Paris, and David Embury (1948) told the best story: a WWI army captain who was driven to the bistro in a motorcycle sidecar. Nobody can prove any of them. Early recipes were equal parts cognac, Cointreau and lemon. Ours adds Pineau des Charentes for extra roundness.
cocktails.notes: I added Pineau des Charentes to the original recipe as I believe it elevates and balances the drink better.

cocktails.name: Garibaldi
cocktails.method: Build - Fluff fresh juices with the milkshake maker, add Campari and Bergamote Liqueur into glass, top with half the juice, add your ice, top with more juice
cocktails.garnish: Orange Wedge
cocktails.tasting_notes: Brunch's favourite bitter. Fluffy fresh orange juice softens Campari's bitter edge, while bergamot liqueur and plum bitters add floral citrus and dark fruit. Light, juicy and very easy to say yes to. Finishes bittersweet with orange and a lingering Campari bite.
cocktails.history: Named after Giuseppe Garibaldi, the general who led the 1860 Expedition of the Thousand and helped unify Italy. The drink is unification in a glass: Campari from the north (Milan) and oranges from the south (Sicily). A long-time Italian bar staple, it got a new lease of life from Naren Young at Dante in New York in the 2010s, where orange juice whipped in a high-speed juicer made it 'fluffy' and famous. We add Briottet bergamot liqueur and plum bitters.

cocktails.name: Dark & Stormy
cocktails.method: Shake ginger syrup and lime juice with ice briefly to awaken both ingredients. Strain into a highball, add some soda to mix it all together. Add a spear, top up with more soda if needed. Float dark rum on top.
cocktails.garnish: Lime Wedge, Angostura Spray
cocktails.tasting_notes: Spicy, dark and bracing. Planteray Dark brings molasses, dried fruit and a little funk, while our ginger syrup gives a proper fiery kick that bottled ginger beer can't match. Lime cuts through and soda keeps it lively. Finishes long and warming with ginger heat and dark sugar.
cocktails.history: Bermuda's national drink, said to have been born after WWI, when Royal Navy sailors started mixing ginger beer from the Dockyard with the local Gosling's Black Seal rum. The name supposedly comes from one sailor, who held it up and declared it 'the colour of a cloud only a fool or a dead man would sail under.' Gosling's owns the trademark (in the US since 1991), so officially a Dark 'n Stormy must use their rum. That's why ours is a Dark & Stormy: Planteray Dark, house ginger syrup, lime and soda.

cocktails.name: Finch Royale
cocktails.method: Build - Add Cognac, cherry liqueur, bitters, and a touch of Champagne to combine. Garnish with the cherry, then top with Champagne.
cocktails.garnish: Jack Rudy Cocktail Cherry
cocktails.tasting_notes: Celebration in a flute. Courvoisier VSOP brings warm dried fruit and oak, Bellamie adds ripe cherry and a hint of marzipan, and orange bitters give it lift. Billecart-Salmon does the rest with fine, toasty bubbles. Finishes crisp and dry with cherry and brioche.
cocktails.history: Our own love child of two Champagne classics. The Champagne Cocktail (sugar, bitters and fizz) was already in Jerry Thomas's 1862 Bar-Tender's Guide, and cognac crept in later. The Kir Royale is the Champagne version of the Kir, named after Canon Félix Kir, the priest and Resistance hero who became mayor of Dijon and served white wine with cassis at every civic do. We keep the cognac and bitters, swap cassis for Bellamie (a modern take on French guignolet cherry liqueur) and top with Billecart-Salmon.

cocktails.name: French 75
cocktails.method: Shake all without champagne, double strain in chilled glass, top with champagne.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon Peel, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: Fizz with a kick. Old Tom gin brings soft botanicals and a touch of sweetness, cognac adds warmth and roundness, and lemon keeps it sharp. Billecart-Salmon lifts it all with elegant bubbles. Finishes dry and zesty with toasty brioche.
cocktails.history: Named after the French 75mm field gun of WWI, because it hits about as hard. Early '75' cocktails were very different: Robert Vermeire's Cocktails: How to Mix Them (1922) had calvados, gin, grenadine and lemon, no fizz at all. The gin, lemon, sugar and Champagne version first appeared as the 'French 75' in Judge Jr.'s Here's How (1927), and the Savoy Cocktail Book (1930) made it famous. Gin or cognac? Bartenders have argued for decades, especially in New Orleans. We settle it by using both.

cocktails.name: Margarita
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with cubed ice, fine strain into guest's choice of glassware, garnish.
cocktails.garnish: Half a salt rim by default unless requested otherwise.
cocktails.tasting_notes: Sharp, salty-sweet and impossible to stop at one. Tapatio Blanco brings bright, peppery cooked agave, Cointreau adds clean orange sweetness and fresh lime makes it snap. Finishes crisp and dry with lime zest and lingering agave.
cocktails.history: Everyone claims it, nobody can prove it. The favourite story credits Carlos 'Danny' Herrera at Rancho La Gloria near Tijuana around 1938, mixing for a showgirl who could only drink tequila. Another credits Dallas socialite Margarita Sames at her Acapulco house in 1948. The likeliest truth is in the name: margarita is Spanish for daisy, and the Daisy (spirit, citrus, orange liqueur) was an old drink family long before anyone added tequila. The first printed Margarita recipe turned up in Esquire in December 1953.
cocktails.notes: When rimming the glass, ensure that you only rim the outside or the glass.

cocktails.name: Matador
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients with Ice, julep strain into chilled glass. Garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon Peel, espressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: A tequila Martini with a twist. Tapatio Reposado brings cooked agave, vanilla and spice, dry vermouth adds herbal crispness and dry curaçao rounds it with bitter orange. A whisper of espadín mezcal brings smoke. Finishes dry and savoury with agave, orange peel and a wisp of smoke.
cocktails.history: Here's the surprise: our Matador is closer to the original than most. It first appeared in the Café Royal Cocktail Book (London, 1937), compiled by William J. Tarling, when tequila was still a novelty in Britain: tequila, dry vermouth and orange curaçao, stirred like a Martini. Trader Vic later reinvented it as a tropical tequila, pineapple and lime drink, and that's the version most people know. We've gone back to the 1937 recipe, with reposado for depth and a dash of Quiquiriqui espadín mezcal for smoke.

cocktails.name: Swimming Finch
cocktails.method: Take bottle out of freezer, pour 75ml in shaker, shake hard with ice for a small amount of time - double strain into frozen glass, garnish
cocktails.garnish: 2 Olives, Lemon Twist cut as a "fish". All "Swimming" in the glass.
cocktails.tasting_notes: Briny, ice-cold and seriously clean. Belvedere Organic gives a smooth, pristine base, a splash of dry vermouth adds herbal edge and pickle juice brings savoury, salty bite. Orange bitters add a little lift. Finishes long and saline with a silky snap.
cocktails.history: Our house dirty Martini, born from the after-parties Charles used to throw at film festivals, where his Martini service became a thing of legend. Belvedere Organic, dry vermouth, orange bitters and a splash of pickle juice, poured as cold as we can get it. The name comes from the garnish: olives and a lemon twist cut into a little fish, all 'swimming' in the glass. Pickle juice instead of olive brine gives it a sharper, more savoury bite than the usual dirty.

cocktails.name: Martini
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients in mixing glass - strain into chilled glass, garnish with guests choice
cocktails.garnish: Lemon twist or Olive, guests choice
cocktails.tasting_notes: The king of cocktails, served bone-cold. Nº3 London Dry brings bold juniper, citrus peel and spice, a splash of dry vermouth adds herbal, winey crispness and orange bitters tie it together. Clean, sharp and silky. Finishes long and dry with juniper and orange oil.
cocktails.history: Nobody knows who made the first one, and anyone who tells you otherwise is guessing. It grew out of the Martinez, a sweet gin-and-vermouth drink first printed in O.H. Byron's Modern Bartender's Guide (1884). The first recipe actually called a 'Martini' appeared in Harry Johnson's Bartender's Manual (1888). Over the next 20 years it dried out: sweet vermouth and Old Tom gave way to dry vermouth, London Dry and orange bitters, which is pretty much what we pour today. Ours is that turn-of-the-century style, just very, very cold.
cocktails.notes: There are many ways to enjoy a martini, and each are very personal. Ask your guest how they would like it! Dirty - add 7.5ml olive brine|Filthy - add 12.5ml olive brine and muddle 1 olive in mixing glass|Wet - 22.5ml Vermouth|50/50 - drop Gin to 35ml, Vermouth to 35ml

cocktails.name: Manhattan Sweet
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients with ice, strain into chilled Nick & Nora glass. Garnish
cocktails.garnish: Maraschino cherry - skewered
cocktails.tasting_notes: The classic, and the one to judge a bar by. Spicy Rittenhouse rye brings pepper and baking spice, our sweet vermouth blend rounds it with dried fruit and herbs, and Angostura ties it all together. Silky, rich and spirit-forward, with a dark cherry finish from the garnish.
cocktails.history: Usually credited to the Manhattan Club in New York in the early 1880s. The famous story about a party thrown there by Jennie Jerome, Winston Churchill's mother, doesn't hold up: she was in England at the time. Early printed recipes, like O.H. Byron's in 1884, were whiskey, sweet vermouth and bitters, and rye was New York's whiskey. Sweet is the original, which is why it's our default.
cocktails.notes: Historically, Manhattans are sweet.

cocktails.name: Martinez
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients with ice in mixing glass, strain into chilled Nick & Nora, Garnish
cocktails.garnish: 1x Skewered Maraschino Cherry
cocktails.tasting_notes: The Martini's sweeter, older uncle. Old Tom gin brings soft, malty botanicals, sweet vermouth adds rich herbal fruit and maraschino gives a cherry-almond twist. Two kinds of bitters keep it balanced. Finishes long and silky with cherry, orange peel and spice.
cocktails.history: The missing link between the Manhattan and the Martini. Its first printed recipe was in O.H. Byron's Modern Bartender's Guide (1884), which simply says it's the same as a Manhattan, but with gin instead of whisky. Jerry Thomas's 1887 edition gave the fuller version, with Old Tom, vermouth, maraschino and bitters. Martinez, California says it invented the drink for a Gold Rush miner, but there's no evidence to back that up. Ours sticks to the 1887 template and adds orange bitters and a dash of dry vermouth for lift.

cocktails.name: Negroni
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients in mixing glass with ice, strain into rocks glass with 1 large ice cube. Garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange Peel, expressed and discarded, Orange Wedge
cocktails.tasting_notes: Bitter, sweet and bold, equal parts. London Dry gin brings juniper backbone, Campari adds bitter orange and rhubarb, and sweet vermouth rounds it out with rich herbal fruit. Finishes long and bittersweet with orange peel and a lingering bitter grip.
cocktails.history: The usual story goes like this. Around 1919, at Caffè Casoni in Florence, Count Camillo Negroni asked bartender Fosco Scarselli to make his Americano stronger, so Scarselli swapped the soda for gin and added an orange slice to tell it apart. Historians still argue over whether Camillo was really a count, and a branch of the French Negroni family has its own claim too. Whoever was first, it's gone on to become one of the world's best-selling cocktails. Ours is the classic equal parts.

cocktails.name: Bijou
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients into mixing glass with ice. Strain into chilled glass. Express lemon peel over and discard. Garnish
cocktails.garnish: Express Lemon Peel over cocktail, discard. Skewered maraschino cherry.
cocktails.tasting_notes: Rich, herbal and jewel-bright. Green Chartreuse brings intense alpine herbs and spice, sweet vermouth adds dark fruit and gin keeps it in line. A touch of dry curaçao and orange bitters add citrus lift. Finishes long, warm and herbaceous with orange peel.
cocktails.history: Bijou is French for jewel, and the usual story is that it's named for three gems: gin for diamond, vermouth for ruby and Chartreuse for emerald. Lovely, but nobody can trace that to the original source. What we do know is that it was in Harry Johnson's New and Improved Bartender's Manual (1900): equal parts gin, Italian vermouth and green Chartreuse, plus orange bitters. It disappeared for most of the 20th century, until the cocktail revival brought it back. Ours dials the gin down and adds curaçao.

cocktails.name: Vieux Carré
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients with ice in mixing glass, strain into chilled glass of choice, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon Peel, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: New Orleans in a glass. Rye brings spice, cognac adds dried fruit and warmth, and sweet vermouth and Benedictine layer on honeyed herbs. Peychaud's and Angostura add anise and clove. Finishes long, rich and spicy with dark fruit and herbs.
cocktails.history: Created by Walter Bergeron, head bartender at the Hotel Monteleone in the French Quarter, and first printed in Stanley Clisby Arthur's Famous New Orleans Drinks and How to Mix 'Em (1937). Vieux Carré ('Old Square') is the old name for the French Quarter itself. The hotel's famous revolving Carousel Bar didn't arrive until 1949, so the drink is older than the bar it's now associated with. Equal parts rye, cognac and sweet vermouth with Benedictine and both bitters, just like ours.

cocktails.name: Adonis
cocktails.method: Sitr all ingredients in mixing glass with ice. Strain into chill coupe. Express orange peel over the drink and discard. garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange Peel, expressed and discarded, skewered olive.
cocktails.tasting_notes: Nutty, dry and quietly brilliant. Palo cortado and amontillado bring roasted almond, salted caramel and savoury depth, and sweet vermouth adds herbal fruit. A touch of PX sweetens it and a dash of Campari gives bite. Low in alcohol, big on flavour. Finishes long and dry with walnut and orange peel.
cocktails.history: Named after Adonis, the 1884 Broadway burlesque starring Henry E. Dixey. It ran for 603 performances, the longest run Broadway had seen at that point. You'll often hear the drink was created at the Waldorf-Astoria that year, but the Waldorf didn't open until 1893. The mix-up comes from The Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Book (1935), which recorded it. Classic is fino or amontillado with sweet vermouth and orange bitters. Ours splits two González Byass sherries and adds PX and Campari.

ingredients.name: Gonzalez Byass Vina AB Amontillado Seco

cocktails.name: Southside
cocktails.method: Slap the mint gently, add to shaker with the rest of ingredients, shake with ice. Double strain into chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Big mint leaf floatin on top of cocktail.
cocktails.tasting_notes: Basically a gin Mojito without the bubbles, and sharper for it. London Dry gin and fresh lime give a crisp sour base, while mint brings cool, green freshness. A touch of salt makes every flavour pop. Finishes bright and clean with mint and lime zest.
cocktails.history: Two origin stories, and neither can be proved. One links it to the Southside Sportsmen's Club, a gentlemen's hunting and fishing club on Long Island. The other says Chicago's South Side gangs drank it during Prohibition to hide rough bootleg gin, which makes a better story than it does history. What we do know is that South Side recipes were in print by the 1910s, and that New York's '21' Club made it a signature. Gin, citrus, sugar and mint, shaken and served up.

cocktails.name: Mojito
cocktails.method: Build into highball glass - slap the mint gently, add with all ingredient excluding soda water. Top the glass with 3/4 of crushed ice, churn to mix all ingredients and dillute. Top with more crushed ice, a splash of soda, and garnish
cocktails.garnish: Fresh Mint Sprig, Lime Wedge, Angostura Spray
cocktails.tasting_notes: Cuba's great cooler. Planteray 3 Stars brings light, fruity rum, fresh lime adds zing and mint, gently pressed with granulated sugar, brings cool, sweet freshness. Soda lengthens it. Finishes crisp and refreshing with mint and lime.
cocktails.history: Rum, lime, sugar and mint had been mixed in Cuba for centuries. The popular link to El Draque, a drink named after Sir Francis Drake, is lovely folklore with very little evidence behind it. By the early 1930s, Havana bar books were printing the Mojito as we know it. La Bodeguita del Medio has a famous sign signed by Hemingway: 'My mojito in La Bodeguita, my daiquiri in El Floridita'. Sadly, it's widely believed to be a fake. Muddle gently: you want mint oils, not lawn clippings.

cocktails.name: Old Fashioned
cocktails.method: Regal Stir all ingredients with ice in mixing glass, strain into chill rock glass with a large rock cube, express the orange peel and garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange Peel, Express over the drink.
cocktails.tasting_notes: The original cocktail, and still the benchmark. Michter's bourbon brings caramel, vanilla and baked fruit, dark sugar syrup adds molasses depth and our house bitters blend brings spice. Orange oils finish it. Finishes long and warm with oak, orange and spice.
cocktails.history: This is what 'cocktail' meant in the first place. In 1806, a New York paper, The Balance and Columbian Repository, defined a cocktail as spirits, sugar, water and bitters. By the 1870s and 80s, bartenders were adding curaçao, absinthe and other extras, so traditionalists started asking for an 'old-fashioned' whiskey cocktail. Louisville's Pendennis Club claims it invented the drink, but the drink is older than the club. Ours is the classic build: bourbon, dark sugar, bitters and orange peel.
cocktails.notes: Can swap Bourbon for Michters Rye for a spicier kick, for Michters Sour Mash for a surprising mix of mellowness and spiciness

cocktails.name: Cosmopolitan
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with Ice, double strain into chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange Peel, Express over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: Tart, pink and still fabulous. Clean vodka carries Cointreau's orange sweetness, fresh lime and a splash of cranberry. Bright, crisp and dangerously drinkable. Finishes dry and zesty with orange peel and tart berry.
cocktails.history: Its 1990s fame started in the 1980s, with several people at once. Cheryl Cook at The Strand in Miami Beach is often credited with an early version around 1985. Toby Cecchini at The Odeon in New York refined it in 1988 with Absolut Citron, Cointreau, fresh lime and cranberry. Earlier 'Cosmopolitan' recipes go back to the 1930s, but with gin and raspberry, so it's a different drink. Then Sex and the City made it a global icon. Ours keeps Cecchini's build with Sapling vodka.

cocktails.name: Pornstar Martini
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with ice, double strain in chilled coupe, seerve with a shot of prosecco on the side
cocktails.garnish: Franciacorta Shot
cocktails.tasting_notes: Loud, tropical and unapologetic. Passion fruit liqueur and syrup lead with juicy, tangy fruit, while pineapple liqueur and juice add sunshine. Lime and lemon bitters keep it sharp, so it's never sickly. Finishes tart and fruity with passion fruit and a citrus snap.
cocktails.history: Created by Douglas Ankrah at Townhouse in Knightsbridge, London, around 2002. He first called it the Maverick Martini, after a club in Cape Town, then renamed it for maximum shock value, and it worked. The original came with a shot of prosecco on the side, meant to cleanse the palate between sips (not to pour in). It went on to become one of the UK's best-selling cocktails. Ankrah, one of the great figures of London's bar scene, died in 2021.
cocktails.notes: Aim for a very silky texture.

cocktails.name: Champs-Élysées
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with ice, double strain into chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon Pell, Express over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: A Sidecar that's been to the Alps. Courvoisier VSOP brings dried fruit and warmth, green Chartreuse adds bold herbal spice and lemon keeps it bright. Angostura and a touch of salt pull it together. Finishes long and herbal with lemon zest and brandy.
cocktails.history: Named after Paris's grandest avenue, and essentially a cognac sour with a splash of Chartreuse. It first appeared in Nina Toye and Arthur H. Adair's Drinks: Long and Short (London, 1925), then in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book (1930). It's in the same family as the Sidecar, but the Chartreuse takes it somewhere far more herbal. A great drink for anyone who likes a Sidecar but wants something more interesting.
cocktails.notes: The correct dilution and aeration is crucial for the deliciousness of the drink.

cocktails.name: Diplomat
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients with ice in mixing glass, strain into chilled coupe, express orange peel and discard, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange peel, expressed and discarded. Skewered Maraschino Cherry.
cocktails.tasting_notes: Light, elegant and dangerously sippable. Dry vermouth leads with crisp, herbal, winey notes, sweet vermouth adds soft fruit and a touch of maraschino brings cherry-almond sweetness. Orange bitters lift it. Low in alcohol, big on finesse. Finishes dry with herbs and orange peel.
cocktails.history: A vermouth cocktail from the days when vermouth was the star, not the sidekick. Two parts dry vermouth to one part sweet, with a dash of maraschino, as printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book (1930). Craddock was English-born, but he'd spent years behind American bars before Prohibition sent him back to London and the Savoy's American Bar. This is the perfect drink for guests who want something grown-up without the full Martini wallop.

cocktails.name: Hickory
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients with ice, strain into chilled coupe glass, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon Peel, express over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: Bittersweet, low and lovely. St-Raphaël Quina Amber brings gentle quinine bitterness and candied orange, sweet vermouth adds rich herbal fruit and a splash of Picon gives a burnt-orange bite. Finishes long and bittersweet with orange peel and herbs.
cocktails.history: First printed in Beverages de Luxe (1911), which says it was 'supposed to be originated by Old General Hickory', meaning Andrew Jackson, and was 'much used in New Orleans'. Jackson died in 1845, decades before cocktails like this existed, so treat that claim with a pinch of salt. The original was half French vermouth, half Italian, plus a teaspoon of Amer Picon. Ours swaps the dry vermouth for St-Raphaël's quinquina, so it's richer and more bitter.

cocktails.name: Whisky Sour
cocktails.method: Dry shake (without ice) all ingredients to emulsiphy the egg, add ice to your shaker and shake hard. Double strain into a chilled glass. Garnish.
cocktails.garnish: Angostura Spray
cocktails.tasting_notes: The sour that made sours famous. Evan Williams bourbon brings caramel and vanilla, fresh lemon adds zing and sugar balances it out. Egg white shakes up into a silky, velvety foam. Angostura on top adds spice. Finishes rounded and tart with lemon and warm bourbon.
cocktails.history: Spirit, citrus and sugar is one of the oldest formulas behind any bar. Sours were already in Jerry Thomas's Bar-Tender's Guide (1862), and the whiskey version was an American staple by the 1870s. The egg white came later. Strictly, a sour with egg white is a 'Boston Sour', but these days most bars add it as standard. Shake dry first, then with ice, to get that thick, silky head.

cocktails.name: Amaretto Sour
cocktails.ice: 1x Large Cube if in rocks glass.
cocktails.method: Dry shake (without ice) all ingredients to emulsiphy the egg, add ice to your shaker and shake hard. Double strain into a chilled glass. Garnish.
cocktails.garnish: Angostura Bitters Spray, Maraschino cherry skewered
cocktails.tasting_notes: A guilty pleasure, made properly. Amaretto brings sweet almond and marzipan, a splash of bourbon adds backbone and fresh lemon keeps it sharp. Egg white makes it silky, and maraschino syrup adds a cherry kiss. Finishes nutty and tart, with none of the sickliness of the 70s version.
cocktails.history: Born in the 1970s, when amaretto (led by Disaronno) took off in the US. The original was amaretto and sour mix, and serious bartenders sneered at it for decades. That changed in 2012, when Jeffrey Morgenthaler of Clyde Common in Portland, Oregon published his fix: add cask-strength bourbon, fresh lemon and egg white. Suddenly, a guilty pleasure became a respectable drink. Ours follows his lead with Evan Williams and adds maraschino syrup.

cocktails.name: Vancouver
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients with ice in mixing glass. Strain into chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange peel, expressed over the drink.
cocktails.tasting_notes: A Martinez with a Canadian passport. London Dry gin brings juniper, Bénédictine adds honey and baking spice, and both vermouths bring herbal, winey depth. Orange bitters tie it together. Finishes long and herbal with honey and orange peel.
cocktails.history: Vancouver's own classic, and it's had two lives. The earliest recipe is in the About Town cocktail book (Vancouver, 1925): gin, French (dry) vermouth, Bénédictine and orange bitters. Later, the Sylvia Hotel, which got the city's first cocktail lounge licence in 1954, made it with sweet vermouth. It vanished in the 60s, until bartender Steve Da Cruz revived it in 2006 after a regular wrote it on a napkin. Dry or sweet? Ours uses both.

cocktails.name: Revolver
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients with ice in mixing glass, strain into chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange Peel, flamed and expressed over drink.
cocktails.tasting_notes: An Old Fashioned that's had an espresso. Evan Williams bourbon brings caramel and oak, coffee liqueur adds roasted, bittersweet depth and a touch of dark sugar rounds it. Orange bitters cut through. Finishes long and warm with coffee, orange oil and vanilla.
cocktails.history: A modern classic from Jon Santer at Bruno's in San Francisco's Mission District, around 2004. The idea is simple: an Old Fashioned built with coffee liqueur and orange bitters, finished with a flamed orange peel. It spread quickly through the American craft cocktail scene and is a great 'next step' for Old Fashioned fans. Ours uses Evan Williams, Black Twist coffee liqueur and a touch of dark sugar.

cocktails.name: Toreador
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with Ice, Double strain into chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lime Wedge over the rim
cocktails.tasting_notes: The Margarita's apricot-loving older sibling. Tapatio Blanco brings bright, peppery agave, apricot liqueur adds juicy stone fruit and fresh lime keeps it zingy. A touch of salt makes it pop. Finishes crisp and fruity with lime and apricot.
cocktails.history: First printed in the Café Royal Cocktail Book (London, 1937), compiled by William J. Tarling, at a time when tequila was barely known outside Mexico. Half tequila, a quarter apricot brandy and a quarter lime or lemon. The same book has the Picador (tequila, Cointreau, lime), which is basically a Margarita 16 years before the Margarita was in print. Bullfighting names were all the rage for tequila drinks back then. Ours is very close to the 1937 spec.

cocktails.name: Charlie Chaplin
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with ice, double strain into chilled coupe.
cocktails.garnish: None
cocktails.tasting_notes: Fruity, tart and a bit cheeky, like the man himself. Sloe gin brings plummy, jammy berry, apricot liqueur adds ripe stone fruit and fresh lime cuts right through. Equal parts and perfectly balanced. Finishes bright and tangy with plum and apricot.
cocktails.history: A pre-Prohibition favourite from the original Waldorf-Astoria in New York, named after the biggest film star of the day. It was recorded in A.S. Crockett's Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Book (1935), which collected the drinks served at the hotel's famous bar before Prohibition closed it. The old hotel was demolished in 1929 to make way for the Empire State Building. Equal parts sloe gin, apricot brandy and lime, exactly as we make it.

cocktails.name: French Pearl
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients - except champagne - with ice, double strain into chilled coupe, top with champagne, garnish
cocktails.garnish: 1 fresh mint leaf floating on top of the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: Fresh, bright and quietly sophisticated. London Dry gin and lemon give a crisp sour base, mint brings cool freshness and a few dashes of absinthe add a whisper of anise. Billecart-Salmon on top adds elegant fizz. Finishes dry and refreshing with mint, lemon and a faint anise trail.
cocktails.history: A modern classic from Audrey Saunders, one of the bartenders who kicked off New York's cocktail revival, created at Bemelmans Bar in the Carlyle Hotel in the early 2000s. Saunders went on to open the hugely influential Pegu Club in 2005. Her original is basically a Southside with a dash of Pernod: gin, citrus, sugar, mint and anise. We make it with La Fée absinthe and finish it with a splash of Champagne.

cocktails.name: Pan American Clipper
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with ice, double strain into chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Maraschino Cherry at the botttom of the glass.
cocktails.tasting_notes: Apple-forward, tart and a little mysterious. Busnel VSOP calvados brings baked apple and oak, lime adds zing and grenadine gives tart pomegranate sweetness. A couple of dashes of absinthe add a herbal, anise lift. Finishes crisp and dry with apple and a hint of anise.
cocktails.history: Named after Pan Am's Clipper flying boats, the height of glamour in 1930s air travel. It comes from Charles H. Baker Jr.'s The Gentleman's Companion (1939), a gloriously eccentric travel-and-drinks memoir. Baker's recipe used applejack, lime, grenadine and absinthe, and it was revived in the 2000s after being rediscovered by modern bartenders. Ours swaps the applejack for French calvados.

cocktails.name: Flora Dora
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients - excluding ginger ale - double strain to chilled glass, top with ginger ale, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lime Wedge, raspberry
cocktails.tasting_notes: Pink, fizzy and full of fun. London Dry gin brings juniper, raspberry liqueur adds juicy berry sweetness and fresh lime keeps it bright. Ginger ale lengthens it with gentle spice. Finishes crisp and refreshing with raspberry and ginger.
cocktails.history: Named after Florodora, the 1899 London musical that became a smash hit on Broadway in 1900, running for over 500 performances. The 'Florodora Girls', a sextet of chorus girls, were the celebrity sensations of the day, and several married millionaires. Like many drinks of that era, the story of who first made it, and for which girl, can't be pinned down. The template is gin, raspberry, lime and ginger, served long. Ours uses Giffard framboise and Fever-Tree ginger ale.

cocktails.name: Rye Sazerac
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients in mixing glass, rinse a chilled rocks glass with absinthe. Strain the cocktail into absinthe-rinsed rocks, express lemon peel over the drink, discard
cocktails.garnish: Absinthe Rinse, Lemon peel expressed over the drink, discarded
cocktails.tasting_notes: Spicy, aromatic and seriously boozy. Rittenhouse rye brings bold spice, Peychaud's adds cherry-anise bitterness and a touch of sugar softens the edges. The absinthe rinse gives a haunting anise perfume. Finishes long and dry with rye spice and lemon oil.
cocktails.history: New Orleans' official cocktail (since 2008). The name comes from Sazerac de Forge et Fils, a cognac imported by the Sazerac Coffee House in the 1850s, served with the bitters of local pharmacist Antoine Peychaud. Phylloxera wiped out French vineyards from the 1870s, so cognac got scarce and rye took over. This is the version most New Orleans bars pour today. The first printed recipe appeared in William Boothby's The World's Drinks (1908). And no, the word 'cocktail' doesn't come from Peychaud's egg cup: it was in print by 1806.

cocktails.name: Cognac Sazerac
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients in mixing glass, rinse a chilled rocks glass with absinthe. Strain the cocktail into absinthe-rinsed rocks, express lemon peel over the drink, discard
cocktails.garnish: Absinthe Rinse, Lemon peel expressed over the drink, discarded
cocktails.tasting_notes: Rounder, richer and softer than its rye cousin. Courvoisier VSOP brings dried fruit, vanilla and oak, Peychaud's adds cherry-anise bitterness and a touch of sugar smooths it. The absinthe rinse brings the trademark anise perfume. Finishes long and elegant with brandy and lemon oil.
cocktails.history: The Sazerac as it's said to have started. The Sazerac Coffee House in New Orleans was named after the cognac it imported, Sazerac de Forge et Fils, and served it with Antoine Peychaud's bitters in the 1850s. Then phylloxera wrecked French vineyards and rye stepped in. Absinthe was banned in the US from 1912 to 2007, so for nearly a century New Orleans used local substitutes like Herbsaint. Ours goes back to the cognac roots with Courvoisier VSOP and a real absinthe rinse.

cocktails.name: Sazerac
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients in mixing glass, rinse a chilled rocks glass with absinthe. Strain the cocktail into absinthe-rinsed rocks, express lemon peel over the drink, discard
cocktails.garnish: Absinthe Rinse, Lemon peel expressed over the drink, discarded
cocktails.tasting_notes: The best of both worlds. Rittenhouse rye brings spice and structure, Courvoisier VSOP adds dried fruit and roundness, and Peychaud's brings cherry-anise bitterness. A touch of sugar and an absinthe rinse finish it off. Finishes long and complex with spice, brandy and lemon oil.
cocktails.history: Why choose? The Sazerac started with cognac in 1850s New Orleans, then switched to rye in the late 1800s when phylloxera destroyed French vineyards. Many modern bars, us included, split the base to get rye's spice and cognac's richness in the same glass. The rest is the classic ritual: sugar, Peychaud's bitters, an absinthe-rinsed glass and a lemon twist (expressed, then discarded). It's been New Orleans' official cocktail since 2008.

cocktails.name: Pendennis Club
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with ice, double strain into a chilled coupe.
cocktails.garnish: Skewered Maraxchino Cherry
cocktails.tasting_notes: Fruity, bright and a little bit fancy. London Dry gin brings juniper, apricot and vine-peach liqueurs add juicy stone fruit and lime keeps it sharp. Peychaud's gives it a pink blush and a cherry-anise edge. Finishes crisp and fruity with apricot and spice.
cocktails.history: The house cocktail of the Pendennis Club, a private gentlemen's club in Louisville, Kentucky, founded in 1881. The classic recipe of gin, apricot brandy, lime and Peychaud's appears in Louisville's own Beverages de Luxe (1911). The same club also claims to have invented the Old Fashioned, which it almost certainly didn't, but this one is genuinely theirs. Ours adds a splash of vine-peach liqueur for extra stone fruit.

ingredients.name: Giffard Crème de Peche de Vigne

cocktails.name: Clover Club
cocktails.method: Dry shake (without ice) all ingredients to emulsiphy the egg, add ice to your shaker and shake hard. Double strain into a chilled glass. Garnish.
cocktails.garnish: Skewered Raspberry
cocktails.tasting_notes: Pink, silky and far tougher than it looks. Gin and lemon give a crisp sour backbone, raspberry liqueur and raspberry oleo bring juicy berry, and dry vermouth adds a winey edge. Egg white whips it into a velvety foam. Finishes tart and fruity with raspberry and lemon.
cocktails.history: Named after the Clover Club, a Philadelphia gentlemen's club of lawyers, writers and businessmen that met at the Bellevue-Stratford Hotel from the 1880s to the 1910s. Recipes were circulating by the early 1900s, and some early ones included dry vermouth, just like ours. It was seen as a 'girly' drink for most of the 20th century, until the cocktail revival brought it back. Julie Reiner even named her Brooklyn bar after it in 2008. Gin, raspberry, lemon and egg white.

cocktails.name: Last Word
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with ice, double strain into chilled Nick & Nora, Garnish
cocktails.garnish: express lime peel over drink and discard, sink Maraschino Cherry
cocktails.tasting_notes: Equal parts, total balance. Green Chartreuse brings intense herbal spice, maraschino adds cherry-almond funk, gin brings juniper and lime keeps it all bright. Sharp, sweet, herbal and sour all at once. Finishes long and herbal with lime and Chartreuse.
cocktails.history: First seen on the Detroit Athletic Club's menu in 1916, priced at 35 cents, the most expensive drink on the list. Vaudeville monologist Frank Fogarty took it to New York, and it was printed in Ted Saucier's Bottoms Up (1951). Then it disappeared, until Murray Stenson put it on the menu at the Zig Zag Café in Seattle around 2004. Bartenders went mad for it. Equal parts gin, green Chartreuse, maraschino and lime, as it's always been.

cocktails.name: Hugo Spritz
cocktails.method: Build in wine glass, elderflower, mint and ice first, Gentle stir, Garnish, top with Franciacorta.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon Wedge, Fresh Mint Sprig
cocktails.tasting_notes: Spring in a glass. Elderflower liqueur brings soft, floral sweetness, fresh mint adds cool, green lift and Franciacorta gives crisp, toasty fizz. Light, fragrant and low in alcohol. Finishes fresh and floral with mint and elderflower.
cocktails.history: A 21st-century spritz from the Alps. Roland 'AK' Gruber created it in 2005 at his San Zeno bar in Naturns, South Tyrol, as a lighter, less bitter alternative to the Aperol Spritz. He nearly called it Otto, then went with Hugo because he liked the sound of it (say it the Italian way: 'Ugo'). His original used lemon balm syrup, but elderflower soon took over because it was much easier to get hold of. Ours keeps it simple: elderflower liqueur, mint and Franciacorta.

cocktails.name: Brandy Alexander
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with ice to combine and cool down. Strain back into small tin and dry shake, this will allow the egg and cream to emulsify. Strain into a chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Grated Nutmeg
cocktails.tasting_notes: Pudding in a glass, and proud of it. Courvoisier VSOP brings warm dried fruit, dark and white crème de cacao add chocolate richness and a whole egg and cream shake into a silky, custardy body. Nutmeg on top. Finishes long and indulgent with chocolate, vanilla and brandy.
cocktails.history: It started life as the gin Alexander, first printed in Hugo Ensslin's Recipes for Mixed Drinks (1916): gin, crème de cacao and cream. Brandy took over by the 1930s, and the brandy version became the go-to after-dinner drink. John Lennon called it his 'milkshake' during his 1974 'Lost Weekend' with Harry Nilsson, and they got thrown out of the Troubadour after a few too many. Ours adds a whole egg for an extra-rich, flip-style texture.

cocktails.name: Classic Champagne Cocktail
cocktails.method: Soak sugar cube with Angostura, drop at the bottom of a chilled coupe. Pour Cognac first, add Champagne slowly
cocktails.garnish: Effervescent, elegant, and celebratory. Warm bitters and caramelised sugar balanced by crisp champagne with a citrus lift.
cocktails.tasting_notes: Pure old-school glamour. A bitters-soaked sugar cube fizzes away at the bottom, sending up a steady stream of bubbles, while cognac adds warmth and dried fruit. Billecart-Salmon brings toasty brioche and crisp acidity. Finishes dry, elegant and gently spiced.
cocktails.history: One of the oldest cocktails there is. Jerry Thomas included a Champagne Cocktail in his Bar-Tender's Guide (1862): a sugar cube, bitters and Champagne, with a twist of lemon. The cognac came later, in the 20th century, and is now pretty much standard. It's the definition of a celebration drink, and the dissolving sugar cube keeps the bubbles going right to the end. Ours uses Courvoisier VSOP and Billecart-Salmon Brut Réserve.

cocktails.name: Corpse Reviver nº1
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients with ice in mixing glass, strain into chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange Peel, Expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: A hair of the dog in a tuxedo. Courvoisier cognac brings dried fruit and warmth, Busnel calvados adds baked apple and sweet vermouth rounds it with rich herbal fruit. Orange bitters lift it. Stirred, strong and smooth. Finishes long with apple, brandy and spice.
cocktails.history: Corpse revivers' were a whole 19th-century category of hangover drinks meant to bring you back from the dead. The Nº1 is from Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book (1930): two parts brandy, one part apple brandy (or calvados) and one part sweet vermouth, 'to be taken before 11am, or whenever steam and energy are needed'. It's always been overshadowed by its gin-based sibling, the Nº2. Ours follows Craddock with Courvoisier and Busnel, plus orange bitters.

cocktails.name: Corpse Reviver Nº2
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with ice, rinse the chilled glass with absinthe. Double Strain into said glass, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon peel, expressed over the drink.
cocktails.tasting_notes: Bright, zesty and dangerously easy. Gin brings juniper, Cointreau adds clean orange sweetness, Cocchi Americano gives a gentle quinine bitterness and fresh lemon keeps it razor-sharp. Equal parts, perfectly balanced. Finishes crisp and dry with citrus peel and a soft bitter edge.
cocktails.history: The more famous of the Savoy's hangover cures. Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book (1930) lists it as equal parts gin, Cointreau, Kina Lillet and lemon, with a dash of absinthe, and warns that 'four of these taken in swift succession will unrevive the corpse again.' Kina Lillet was reformulated in 1986 and lost most of its quinine bite, which is why many bars, including us, use Cocchi Americano to get closer to the original taste.

cocktails.name: East-8 Hold Up
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients together with cubed ice, fine strain over ice, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lime Wedge
cocktails.tasting_notes: Tropical, bittersweet and crowd-pleasing. Clean vodka carries juicy pineapple and tangy passion fruit, Aperol adds bitter orange and rhubarb and lime keeps it zippy. Finishes fruity and refreshing with a gentle bitter twist.
cocktails.history: A modern London classic from Kevin Armstrong at Milk & Honey in Soho, created around 2010. The name has a great story: Armstrong dropped a friend off in E8 (Hackney), and the friend got mugged while answering the call of nature in the street, trousers down. Armstrong named a drink after it. Vodka, Aperol, pineapple, lime and passion fruit. Proof that even bad nights can lead to good drinks.
cocktails.notes: Aim for a nice fluffy head from the pineapple juice.

cocktails.name: Satan's Whiskers
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with ice, double strain into chilled coupe. Garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange Peel, expressed over the drink.
cocktails.tasting_notes: A Bronx with a wicked streak. Gin brings juniper, dry vermouth adds herbal crispness and Cocchi Dopo Teatro brings bittersweet, chocolatey depth. Fresh orange juice and curaçao turn it juicy, and orange bitters tie it together. Finishes bittersweet with orange and herbs.
cocktails.history: From Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), in two styles. 'Straight' uses Grand Marnier, while 'Curled' uses orange curaçao. Both are equal parts gin, French and Italian vermouth and orange juice, plus a half-measure of orange liqueur and orange bitters. In other words, it's a Bronx with extra orange liqueur. Nobody knows where the devilish name came from. Ours is 'curled' (curaçao), with Cocchi Dopo Teatro in place of the sweet vermouth for extra bitterness.

cocktails.name: Bronx
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with ice, Double Strain into chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange Peel, expressed over the drink.
cocktails.tasting_notes: A Perfect Martini that's had breakfast. Gin brings juniper, sweet and dry vermouth bring herbal, winey depth and fresh orange juice makes it juicy and bright. Orange bitters tie it together. Finishes crisp and orangey with herbs.
cocktails.history: Credited to Johnny Solon at the old Waldorf-Astoria around 1900. As the story goes, he'd just visited the Bronx Zoo and named the drink after the strange beasts drinkers claim to see after a few too many. By the 1930s it was one of America's most-ordered cocktails, up there with the Martini and the Manhattan. Then it fell out of fashion, and you hardly ever see it now. Ours uses both vermouths, which technically makes it a 'Perfect' Bronx.

cocktails.name: White Negroni
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients with ice in mixing glass, strain into chilled rock glass over large cube, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon Peel, Expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: A Negroni's pale, French cousin. Old Tom gin brings soft botanicals, Dolin Blanc adds floral, honeyed sweetness and gentian amer brings earthy, bitter bite. Bergamot liqueur adds Earl Grey-style citrus. Finishes long, bitter and floral with bergamot and gentian.
cocktails.history: Created by British bartender Wayne Collins in 2001, while he was at VinExpo in Bordeaux with Nick Blacknell. Short of Italian ingredients, they made it with what they had: Plymouth gin, Lillet Blanc and Suze, a French gentian liqueur. The result is a bittersweet, golden Negroni that's become a modern classic in its own right. Ours keeps the French theme with Dolin Blanc and Grandmont gentian amer, and adds bergamot.

cocktails.name: French Martini
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with ice, strain into chiled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Raspberry Powder
cocktails.tasting_notes: Fruity, frothy and very 90s, in the best way. Clean vodka carries juicy raspberry liqueur, while pineapple juice adds tropical sweetness and shakes into a silky foam. Finishes smooth and fruity with raspberry and pineapple.
cocktails.history: Not French and not a Martini. It's usually credited to Keith McNally's Pravda bar in SoHo, New York, which opened in 1996, and it rode the 90s 'anything-in-a-V-glass-is-a-Martini' wave. The 'French' bit comes from Chambord, the black raspberry liqueur from the Loire Valley, which the drink was built around. Shake hard so the pineapple froths up. Ours swaps the Chambord for Giffard crème de framboise.

cocktails.name: Tom Collins
cocktails.method: Build in highball, add all ingredients, add ice, top with more soda If necessary, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon Wedge
cocktails.tasting_notes: The original long, cold gin drink. Old Tom gin brings soft, slightly sweet botanicals, lemon adds bright zing and sugar balances it. Soda water lengthens it into a crisp, sparkling refresher. Finishes clean and zesty with lemon and gentle juniper.
cocktails.history: It probably started with John Collins, a head waiter at Limmer's Hotel in London, famous for his gin punch in the early 1800s. In 1874, the 'Tom Collins hoax' swept New York: people told friends that a man called Tom Collins had been bad-mouthing them in a nearby bar, sending them off to find someone who didn't exist. Bartenders cashed in with a drink of the same name. Jerry Thomas printed it in 1876. Old Tom gin was the original, as in ours.

cocktails.name: Airmail
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients (exept Champagne) with ice, double strain into chilled and iced Highball, top with Champagne, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Fresh Mint Sprig, Lime Wedge
cocktails.tasting_notes: A Daiquiri that's gone first class. Planteray 3 Stars brings light, fruity rum, fresh lime adds zing and honey gives a rounded, floral sweetness. Billecart-Salmon on top adds toasty fizz, and Angostura a touch of spice. Finishes dry and bright with honey and lime.
cocktails.history: A rum-and-Champagne drink from the golden age of air travel, named after the airmail flights that linked the US and the Caribbean. Its first known printed recipe is in Esquire's Handbook for Hosts (1949): rum, lime and honey, topped with Champagne. Think of it as a cross between a honey Daiquiri and a French 75. It was largely forgotten until the craft cocktail revival brought it back. Ours adds a dash of Angostura for spice.

cocktails.name: Spring Feeling
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with ice, double strain into chilled coupe. Garnish
cocktails.garnish: Skewered Maraschino Cherry
cocktails.tasting_notes: Fresh, green and herbal. London Dry gin brings juniper, green Chartreuse adds a big hit of alpine herbs and spice, and fresh lemon keeps it bright. A touch of sugar softens the edges. Finishes long and herbal with lemon zest.
cocktails.history: Straight out of Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book (1930): gin, green Chartreuse and lemon, two parts to one to one. It's basically a Last Word without the maraschino, so it's drier, sharper and more about the Chartreuse. A forgotten gem that's perfect for herbal-drink lovers. We add a touch of sugar to take the edge off.

cocktails.name: Fanciulli
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients with ice in mixing glass, strain into chilled N&N with a Jack Rudy cherry at the bottom
cocktails.garnish: Orange peel, expressed and discarded. Jack Rudy Cherry
cocktails.tasting_notes: A Manhattan with a bitter twist. Rye and bourbon bring spice, caramel and oak, sweet vermouth adds rich herbal fruit and Fernet-Branca brings a cool, minty, bitter bite. A pinch of salt ties it together. Finishes long and bitter with mint, spice and dark fruit.
cocktails.history: Named after Francesco Fanciulli, the Italian-born conductor who took over from John Philip Sousa as leader of the US Marine Band (1892–97). The recipe is in A.S. Crockett's Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Book (1935): whiskey, sweet vermouth and Fernet-Branca, basically a Manhattan with Fernet instead of Angostura. Why name it after a bandleader? Nobody knows. Ours splits the base between Rittenhouse rye and Evan Williams bourbon.

cocktails.name: Paloma
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients except Grapefruit Soda with ice, rim a highball with salt and add an ice spear, strain cocktail into glass, top with grapefruit soda, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Salt, Rim, Long Grapefruit Peel along the spear
cocktails.tasting_notes: Mexico's real favourite. Tapatio Blanco brings bright, peppery agave, fresh grapefruit and lime give tart citrus and agave syrup softens it. Pink grapefruit soda lengthens it, and a touch of salt makes every flavour pop. Finishes crisp and refreshing with grapefruit and agave.
cocktails.history: Paloma means 'dove', and in Mexico it outsells the Margarita by a mile. Its origins are murky. It probably took off after grapefruit sodas like Squirt arrived in Mexico in the 1950s, and tequila and grapefruit soda over ice became an everyday drink. Don Javier Delgado Corona of La Capilla in Tequila is often credited, but his real claim to fame is the Batanga. Ours uses fresh grapefruit and lime topped with pink grapefruit soda, rather than soda alone.

cocktails.name: Pimm's Jug
cocktails.method: Build in Carafe - Ice and fruits first, Pimm's and lemonade after, not over the neck
cocktails.garnish: 1.5 Strawberries cut in quarters by the length, 5 Slices cucumber by the diagonal, 5 fine wedges of orange, and 12 fresh mint leaves.
cocktails.tasting_notes: Summer in England, in a jug. Pimm's Nº1 brings bittersweet orange, spice and gentle herbal notes, and lemonade adds sweet, fizzy citrus. Fresh fruit, cucumber and mint make it fragrant and refreshing. Finishes light and fruity with orange, cucumber and mint.
cocktails.history: Created by James Pimm, a farmer's son from Kent who ran an oyster bar in the City of London in the 1820s. He served a gin-based 'house cup' flavoured with quinine and a secret mix of herbs and spices, and the recipe is still secret today. Pimm's Nº1 Cup was the gin-based one, and the only one that survived (the others used whisky, brandy, rum and so on). Now it's the official drink of Wimbledon and every English summer. One part Pimm's to three parts lemonade, plus fruit and mint.

cocktails.name: Muddy
cocktails.method: Shaken and Layered - Layer first Vodka on the bottom of the glass, then layer with Coole Swan. Shake the rest of ingredients and layer on top of the rest of the drink.
cocktails.garnish: Dusted Choco Powder
cocktails.tasting_notes: Dessert and nightcap in one. Coole Swan Irish cream brings silky cream and white chocolate, coffee and coffee liqueur add roasted bitterness, and vodka and cognac give it backbone. Mole bitters bring a hint of chocolate and spice. Finishes rich and smooth with coffee, cocoa and cream.
cocktails.history: Our own creamy coffee cocktail, from the same family as the White Russian and the Mudslide. The Mudslide is said to have been born at the Wreck Bar at Rum Point on Grand Cayman in the 1970s, when a guest asked for a White Russian and the bar only had Irish cream. The Muddy takes that idea, adding Coole Swan Irish cream, fresh coffee and a splash of cognac, with mole bitters for a spicy chocolate finish.

cocktails.name: Bramble
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients except crème de mure - dump, top with crushed ice, sink crème de mûre, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon wedge
cocktails.tasting_notes: A British hedgerow in a glass. London Dry gin and lemon give a crisp, tart base, and crème de mûre drizzled over crushed ice bleeds through like blackberry juice. Finishes fresh and fruity with blackberry and lemon zest.
cocktails.history: Created by Dick Bradsell in 1984 at Fred's Club in Soho. He wanted a truly British drink, and drew on childhood memories of blackberrying on the Isle of Wight. It's basically a gin sour served over crushed ice, with crème de mûre (blackberry liqueur) drizzled on top so it bleeds down through the ice. Bradsell, the godfather of London's cocktail revival, also gave us the Espresso Martini. One of the few modern British cocktails to become a true global classic.

cocktails.name: Brigadoon
cocktails.method: Shake and double strain
cocktails.garnish: None
cocktails.tasting_notes: A Scotch sour on a tropical holiday. Cutty Sark 12 brings honeyed malt and gentle oak, apricot liqueur adds juicy stone fruit and orgeat gives nutty, almond richness. Lemon keeps it sharp and Angostura adds spice. Finishes long and fruity with apricot, almond and malt.
cocktails.history: A modern Scotch sour credited to Adam McGurk at The Player in Soho, London, the bar where Dick Bradsell also worked. Beyond that, very little has been written about it. It takes a whisky sour and gives it the tiki treatment with apricot and orgeat, a pairing more often seen with rum. The name comes from Brigadoon, the 1947 Broadway musical about a magical Scottish village that appears for only one day every hundred years.

cocktails.name: Mezcal Negroni
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients in mixng glass, strain in rocks glass, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange Peel, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: The Negroni goes to Oaxaca. Quiquiriqui espadín mezcal brings smoky, earthy agave, Campari adds bitter orange and sweet vermouth rounds it with rich herbal fruit. Equal parts and bold. Finishes long and smoky-bittersweet with orange peel.
cocktails.history: A modern twist on the 1919 Florentine classic. Swapping gin for mezcal took off in the 2000s and 2010s, as artisanal mezcal hit bars around the world and bartenders discovered that smoke and Campari are a match made in heaven. It's now a standard on menus everywhere. Same equal-parts formula as the original, just with Quiquiriqui espadín, a mezcal from Oaxaca, in place of gin.

cocktails.name: Bellini
cocktails.method: Add purée and liqueur to a shaker tin, pour a small amount of Franciacorta to mix all ingredients together. Pour mixture into a dessert wine glass, top gently with Franciacorta
cocktails.garnish: None
cocktails.tasting_notes: Peaches and fizz, nothing more needed. White peach purée brings soft, juicy, floral fruit, peach liqueur deepens it and Franciacorta adds crisp, toasty bubbles. Light, elegant and pretty in pink. Finishes fresh and fruity with ripe peach.
cocktails.history: Created by Giuseppe Cipriani at Harry's Bar in Venice, usually dated to 1948. He loved Italy's fragrant white summer peaches, and puréed them with prosecco. The drink's pink glow reminded him of a toga in a painting by the 15th-century Venetian artist Giovanni Bellini, so he named it after him. Harry's Bar, which also gave the world carpaccio, still makes it only when white peaches are in season. Ours uses Franciacorta and adds peach liqueur, so it's good all year round.

ingredients.name: Giffard Crème de Peche de Vigne

cocktails.name: Campari Spritz
cocktails.method: Build in wine glass, Campari first, ice, garnish, straw, and top up with Franciacorta
cocktails.garnish: Orange Wedge
cocktails.tasting_notes: The Aperol Spritz's bolder, more bitter big brother. Campari brings bitter orange, rhubarb and spice, and crisp Franciacorta adds toasty fizz. More bite than an Aperol Spritz, but just as refreshing. Finishes dry and bitter with orange peel.
cocktails.history: The spritz started in the 19th-century Veneto, when Austrian soldiers added a 'spritz' (splash) of water to the strong local wine. Gaspare Campari created his bitter in Novara in 1860 and moved to Milan soon after, and over time the bitters crept into the spritz. In Venice, ordering a 'Spritz Campari' is just as common as Aperol, and many locals consider it the proper one. Ours skips the soda and goes straight for Franciacorta.

cocktails.name: Sbagliato
cocktails.method: Build in rocks glass, add all ingredients except Franciacorta, add ice, give it a quick stir, garnish, and top up with Franciacorta
cocktails.garnish: Orange Wedge
cocktails.tasting_notes: The happiest accident in cocktail history. Campari brings bitter orange, sweet vermouth adds rich herbal fruit and Franciacorta replaces the gin with crisp, toasty fizz. Lighter than a Negroni, but just as bittersweet. Finishes dry and bitter with orange peel.
cocktails.history: Sbagliato means 'mistaken' in Italian. The story goes that at Bar Basso in Milan around 1972, bartender Mirko Stocchetto reached for gin to make a Negroni and grabbed spumante instead. The customer loved it, and a classic was born. Stocchetto, who had trained at Harry's Bar in Venice, ran Bar Basso for decades, and his son Maurizio still runs it. In 2022 it went viral when actor Emma D'Arcy ordered 'a Negroni Sbagliato with prosecco in it'.

cocktails.name: Low ABV Gin Elderflower Spritz
cocktails.method: Build in spritz glass, gin and elderflower
cocktails.garnish: Lemon Wedge and Mint Sprig
cocktails.tasting_notes: Light, floral and easy to love. Alcohol-free elderflower brings soft, fragrant sweetness, a splash of London Dry gin adds a hint of juniper and Franciacorta gives crisp fizz. Fresh mint lifts it. Finishes clean and fresh with elderflower and mint.
cocktails.history: Our own low-ABV spritz for guests who want something lighter. It's inspired by the Hugo, the elderflower spritz created in 2005 by Roland Gruber in Naturns, South Tyrol. We use Giffard's alcohol-free elderflower, just a splash of Haymans gin for backbone, Franciacorta and fresh mint. That keeps it much lower in alcohol than a standard spritz, without losing any of the flavour.

cocktails.name: Espresso Martini (Finch's Style)
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients together (Rum + Mix + Coffee), double strain into coupe. Garnish
cocktails.garnish: chocolate powder line, on a side, fleur de lys design
cocktails.tasting_notes: Our dessert-leaning take on the classic. Planteray Cut & Dry coconut rum brings toasted coconut, while vanilla, white crème de cacao and coffee liqueur add creamy sweetness and chocolate. Fresh double espresso gives the bitter backbone and a thick crema. Finishes rich and smooth with coffee, coconut and vanilla.
cocktails.history: Our house riff on Dick Bradsell's Espresso Martini, which he created around 1983 at the Soho Brasserie in London (the full story is under the classic Espresso Martini). Where Bradsell's original is vodka-sharp, ours goes richer and rounder: Planteray Cut & Dry coconut rum in place of vodka, plus vanilla liqueur and white crème de cacao. It's more of a dessert, with the same wake-up kick.
cocktails.notes: All liqueurs are prebatched together - use the liqueur mix

cocktails.name: Naked & Famous
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients and double strain into N&N. Garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lime Peel
cocktails.tasting_notes: Smoky, bittersweet and wildly balanced. Espadín mezcal brings smoke and earthy agave, Aperol adds bitter orange and rhubarb, yellow Chartreuse gives honeyed herbs and lime keeps it sharp. Equal parts. Finishes long and smoky with orange, honey and lime.
cocktails.history: Created by Joaquín Simó at Death & Co in New York's East Village around 2011. He called it the 'bastard love child' of two other equal-parts drinks: the Last Word (1916) and Sam Ross's modern classic, the Paper Plane. Mezcal replaces the bourbon, yellow Chartreuse the Amaro Nonino, and Aperol stays. Death & Co, opened on New Year's Eve 2006, was one of the bars that defined the cocktail revival. Equal parts of all four, exactly as Simó made it.

cocktails.name: SR VK Martini
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients in mixing glass - strain into chilled glass, garnish with guests choice
cocktails.garnish: Lemon twist or Olive, guests choice
cocktails.tasting_notes: Clean, crisp and ice-cold. Sapling vodka brings smooth, gentle wheat sweetness, and a splash of dry vermouth adds a light herbal, winey edge. Simple, pure and very cold. Finishes clean and dry with a soft, creamy texture.
cocktails.history: Our house Vodka Martini, built on Sapling, a British wheat vodka. Vodka Martinis took off in America in the 1950s and 60s, when vodka was marketed hard as the clean, modern alternative to gin. James Bond made 'shaken, not stirred' famous, though purists will tell you stirring gives a silkier, clearer drink. We keep it simple: Sapling and a splash of dry vermouth, as cold as we can get it.

cocktails.name: Brown Derby (Finch's Style)
cocktails.garnish: Rosemary Sprig
cocktails.tasting_notes: Bright, honeyed and grown-up. Evan Williams bourbon brings caramel and vanilla, fresh grapefruit adds tart, bitter citrus and rosemary honey gives floral, herbal sweetness. A whisper of Ardbeg adds smoke, and plum bitters dark fruit. Finishes crisp and herbal with grapefruit, honey and a wisp of peat.
cocktails.history: A product of 1930s Hollywood, credited to the Vendôme Club on Sunset Boulevard and named after the Brown Derby, the famous hat-shaped restaurant down the road. The classic is just bourbon, grapefruit and honey, and it's basically the same drink as the De Rigueur in Judge Jr.'s Here's How (1927). Ours adds rosemary to the honey, a whisper of smoky Ardbeg and plum bitters, for a more herbal, layered take.

cocktails.name: Passion Toreador
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with cubed ice, fine strain into a chilled coupe
cocktails.tasting_notes: Tropical, smoky and zingy. Tapatio Blanco brings bright, peppery agave, a splash of mezcal adds smoke, and passion fruit liqueur brings tangy, juicy fruit. Lime keeps it sharp and agave softens it. Finishes crisp and fruity with passion fruit and a wisp of smoke.
cocktails.history: Our own riff on the Toreador, a tequila sour first printed in the Café Royal Cocktail Book (London, 1937): tequila, apricot brandy and lime. We swap the apricot for Giffard passion fruit liqueur and add a splash of Quiquiriqui espadín mezcal for smoke. It keeps the original's simple, sharp structure, but goes tropical. Basically a Toreador on holiday in Oaxaca.

cocktails.name: Americano
cocktails.method: Build in highball, Vermouth and Campari and a touch of soda, ice, stir briefly to combine, top soda, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange Wedge
cocktails.tasting_notes: The Negroni's lighter, fizzier parent. Campari brings bitter orange and rhubarb, sweet vermouth adds rich herbal fruit and soda lengthens it into a long, refreshing aperitivo. Low in alcohol and very easy to drink. Finishes bittersweet and crisp with orange peel.
cocktails.history: It started in the 1860s as the 'Milano-Torino' at Gaspare Campari's café in Milan: Campari from Milan and sweet vermouth from Turin. Adding soda made it longer and lighter. The popular story is that it got renamed for the American tourists who loved it, but nobody really knows. What's certain is that it's the parent of the Negroni (gin replaced the soda around 1919), and it's the first drink James Bond orders in Casino Royale (1953).

cocktails.name: Aviation
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients except Crème de Violette, fine strain into a chilled coupe, add you cherry, sink Violette gently and express lemon
cocktails.garnish: Lemon twist, expressed over the drink and discarded, maraschino cherry
cocktails.tasting_notes: Sky-blue and floral. London Dry gin brings juniper, maraschino adds cherry-almond funk, fresh lemon keeps it bright and crème de violette brings a soft floral note and that pale lilac colour. Finishes dry and floral with lemon and violet.
cocktails.history: Created by Hugo Ensslin, head bartender at the Hotel Wallick in New York, and first printed in his Recipes for Mixed Drinks (1916), the last big cocktail book before Prohibition. Its name and pale sky colour celebrated the new age of flight. The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930) left out the crème de violette, so for decades it was made without it, and was grey. Once violette came back to the US in 2007, the original sky-blue Aviation returned.

cocktails.name: Panamerican Clipper
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with cubed ice, fine strain into chilled coupe
cocktails.garnish: None
cocktails.tasting_notes: Apple-forward, tart and a little mysterious. Busnel VSOP calvados brings baked apple and oak, plenty of lime adds zing and pomegranate syrup gives tart, fruity sweetness. A few dashes of absinthe add a herbal, anise lift. Finishes crisp and dry with apple and anise.
cocktails.history: Named after Pan Am's Clipper flying boats, the height of glamour in 1930s air travel. It's from Charles H. Baker Jr.'s The Gentleman's Companion (1939): applejack, lime, grenadine and absinthe. This spec is sharper than our other Pan American Clipper, with more lime and Monin pomegranate syrup in place of grenadine. Grenadine was originally made from pomegranate, after all (grenade is French for pomegranate).

cocktails.name: Vancouver (Finch's Style)
cocktails.method: Regal stir all ingredients excluding Soda water with cubed ice, strain in your highball, add a touch of soda water, ice, soda to top if necessary, garnish
cocktails.garnish: lightly charred Cinammon Stick
cocktails.tasting_notes: The Vancouver, stretched out. London Dry gin brings juniper, Bénédictine adds honey and baking spice and both vermouths bring herbal, winey depth. Orange bitters tie it together, and a soda top makes it longer and lighter. Finishes crisp and herbal with honey and orange peel.
cocktails.history: Our long version of the Vancouver cocktail. The original is in Vancouver's About Town cocktail book (1925), made with dry vermouth, and the Sylvia Hotel later served it with sweet vermouth from 1954 (see the classic Vancouver for the full story). We split the vermouths, push the Bénédictine up a little and top it with soda. That turns a stirred, boozy sipper into something you can drink all evening.

cocktails.name: Between the Sheets
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients together with crushed ice, fine strain into a chilled coupe, garnish.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon Twist, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: A Sidecar with a rum chaser. Courvoisier VSOP brings dried fruit and warmth, Planteray 3 Stars adds light, fruity rum and dry curaçao brings bitter orange. A small hit of lemon keeps it sharp. Strong and smooth. Finishes long and warm with orange peel and brandy.
cocktails.history: A cheeky name for a Sidecar with rum in it. Usually credited to Harry MacElhone at Harry's New York Bar in Paris in the 1920s, it was printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book (1930): equal parts brandy, white rum and Cointreau, with a dash of lemon. The name was supposedly a nod to what the drink might lead to. Ours uses Courvoisier, Planteray 3 Stars and Pierre Ferrand dry curaçao.
cocktails.notes: There are 3 versions of this drink, but only one really braved the ages - much like the Corpse Reviver. This one is the latest (Nº3)and most popular. London Dry Gin subs either Brandy for Nº1, or Rum for Nº2.

cocktails.name: Black Russian
cocktails.method: Stir in mixing glass with cubed ice, strain into your chlled rocks glass over ice
cocktails.garnish: Traditionally none - can offer Maraschino Cherry to guest, brings a nice fruity sweetness that compliments the coffee liqueur
cocktails.tasting_notes: Dark, simple and strong. Black Cow vodka, made from milk, brings a soft, creamy smoothness, and Black Twist coffee liqueur adds roasted coffee and sweetness. Two ingredients, no fuss. Finishes smooth and rich with dark coffee.
