cocktails.history: Created in 1949 by Gustave Tops, the barman at the Hotel Metropole in Brussels, for Perle Mesta, the American ambassador to Luxembourg. The name is simple: it's dark, and vodka is Russia's spirit. Add cream and it becomes a White Russian, which The Big Lebowski made famous. Ours uses Black Cow, a Dorset vodka distilled from cows' milk whey, which gives it an extra-smooth, creamy texture.
cocktails.notes: Any vodka work, but I find that the creamy texture of black cow really elevates that simple drink.

cocktails.name: Stonecutter
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients together with ice, Strain into a Rocks Glass, add your large cube, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange Coin
cocktails.tasting_notes: Dark, smoky and spirit-forward. Reposado tequila brings cooked agave and vanilla, espadín mezcal adds earthy smoke and dark crème de cacao brings rich chocolate. Black walnut and mole bitters add nutty, spicy depth. Finishes long and smoky with cocoa and toasted nut.
cocktails.history: An agave Old Fashioned in the style of the Oaxaca Old Fashioned, which Phil Ward created at Death & Co in New York around 2007: reposado tequila, mezcal, a touch of sweetness and bitters. We haven't found a published original for the Stonecutter itself, so treat this as our spec. It splits tequila and mezcal equally and uses dark crème de cacao in place of agave syrup, with black walnut and mole bitters to bring out the chocolate.

cocktails.name: Blood and Sands
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with cubed ice, fine strain into a chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Skewered Maraschino Cherry
cocktails.tasting_notes: Fruity, rich and a touch smoky. Cutty Sark 12 brings honeyed malt, Bellamie cherry liqueur adds ripe cherry and marzipan and sweet vermouth gives rich herbal fruit. Fresh orange juice brightens it, and a whisper of Ardbeg adds peat. Finishes long and fruity with cherry, orange and a wisp of smoke.
cocktails.history: Named after Blood and Sand, the 1922 film that starred Rudolph Valentino as a Spanish bullfighter. It was first printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book (1930): equal parts Scotch, cherry brandy, sweet vermouth and orange juice. It's one of very few classic cocktails built on Scotch, and the red of the cherry is said to stand for the blood. Ours swaps Cherry Heering for Bellamie and adds a splash of Ardbeg for smoke.

cocktails.name: Bloody Mary
cocktails.method: Roll all ingredients together, pour into highball, ice and garnish
cocktails.garnish: Skewered Cucumber, Lemon Wedge and Olive, Cracked Black Pepper
cocktails.tasting_notes: Savoury, spicy and the ultimate hair of the dog. Sapling vodka gives a clean base, while tomato juice and our Mary Mix bring savoury richness, spice and heat. Fresh lemon keeps it bright. Finishes long and savoury with pepper, spice and tomato.
cocktails.history: Fernand 'Pete' Petiot said he invented it at Harry's New York Bar in Paris in the early 1920s, mixing vodka and tomato juice. Entertainer George Jessel also claimed it, around 1927. Petiot then moved to the St. Regis Hotel in New York in 1934, spiced it up with salt, pepper, lemon and Worcestershire, and briefly renamed it the Red Snapper. Nobody knows who 'Mary' was. Ours is made with Sapling vodka and our own Mary Mix.

cocktails.name: Bullshot
cocktails.method: Roll all ingredients together, pour into highball, ice and garnish
cocktails.garnish: Skewered Lemon Wedge and Olive, Cracked Black Pepper
cocktails.tasting_notes: A Bloody Mary that's had a steak. Sapling vodka gives a clean base, while beef consommé brings deep, savoury, meaty richness and our Mary Mix adds spice and heat. Fresh lemon keeps it bright. Finishes long and savoury with beef, pepper and spice.
cocktails.history: A 1950s American curiosity, usually credited to Lester Gruber's Caucus Club in Detroit, where it was reportedly dreamed up with executives from the Campbell Soup Company, who were trying to sell more canned beef consommé. Basically a Bloody Mary with beef stock instead of tomato. It was a big hangover cure at mid-century brunches, and it's having a bit of a comeback. Ours uses Sapling vodka, beef consommé and our Mary Mix.
cocktails.allergens: Fish, Gluten, Celery, Mustard, Sulphites, Celery

cocktails.name: Brooklyn
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients together with cubed ice, strain into a chiled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Skewered Maraschino Cherry
cocktails.tasting_notes: The Manhattan's drier, more mysterious sibling. Rittenhouse rye brings spice, dry vermouth adds crisp herbal notes, maraschino gives a cherry-almond twist and Picon brings bitter, burnt orange. Finishes long and dry with rye spice, orange peel and cherry.
cocktails.history: One of the borough cocktails, first printed in Jacob Grohusko's Jack's Manual (1908): rye, dry vermouth, maraschino and Amer Picon. Picon stopped being exported to the US, so for decades the Brooklyn was almost impossible to make properly, which is why the Manhattan stayed famous while it faded away. In the 2000s, New York bartenders started a whole wave of neighbourhood riffs on it, like the Red Hook and the Greenpoint. Ours is the 1908 classic, with real Picon.

cocktails.name: Caipirinha
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients together, dump into a rocks glass, top with a small crushed ice mount, garnish
cocktails.garnish: 2 lime wedges
cocktails.tasting_notes: Brazil's national drink, rough and ready in the best way. Velho Barreiro cachaça brings grassy, funky sugarcane, while fresh lime wedges muddled with caster sugar release juice and bitter peel oils. Served over crushed ice. Finishes zesty, sweet and tart with lime and cane.
cocktails.history: Brazil's national cocktail, made with cachaça, a spirit distilled from fresh sugarcane juice. A popular story says it started as a flu remedy in São Paulo state around 1918 (lime, garlic and honey), but there's very little evidence for it. The name comes from 'caipira', meaning country folk. Brazil even defined the recipe in law in 2003: cachaça, lime and sugar. Muddle the lime wedges to get the oils out of the peel, but don't overdo it, or the pith turns bitter.

cocktails.name: Caipiroska
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients together, dump into a rocks glass, top with a small crushed ice mount, garnish
cocktails.garnish: 2 limes wedges
cocktails.tasting_notes: The Caipirinha's cleaner, smoother cousin. Sapling vodka gives a neutral base, while fresh lime wedges muddled with caster sugar bring juice and zesty peel oils. Served over crushed ice. Finishes crisp, sweet and tart with lime.
cocktails.history: Simply a Caipirinha made with vodka instead of cachaça. It's popular in Brazil itself, and caught on across Europe in the 1990s and 2000s, when cachaça was still hard to find outside Brazil. The 'roska' bit is a nod to vodka's Russian roots. Same technique as the Caipirinha: muddle lime wedges with sugar, add crushed ice and spirit. It's a good option for guests who find cachaça too funky.

cocktails.name: Cantarito
cocktails.method: Build in chilled highball glass, give a quick stir, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lime Wedge
cocktails.tasting_notes: Jalisco's party drink. Tapatio Reposado brings cooked agave and gentle spice, while fresh orange, grapefruit and lime give a big, juicy citrus hit. A pinch of Maldon salt and pink grapefruit soda make it bright and fizzy. Finishes long and refreshing with citrus and agave.
cocktails.history: Named after the small clay pots (cántaros) it's traditionally served in, which keep the drink cold. The Cantarito is a roadside favourite in Jalisco, especially around the town of Tequila and Amatitán, where stands mix it in huge batches, often in clay pots, for weekend crowds. Tequila, fresh orange, grapefruit and lime, a pinch of salt, topped with grapefruit soda. Think of it as a Paloma with extra fruit. We use Tapatio Reposado.

cocktails.name: Hemingway Daiquiri
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients together with ice, fine strain into a chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lime Peel, expressed over drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: A Daiquiri with a sharper, drier edge. Planteray 3 Stars brings light, fruity rum, lime and grapefruit add tart, bitter citrus and maraschino gives a cherry-almond twist. Just a touch of sugar. Finishes bright, dry and zesty with grapefruit and lime.
cocktails.history: Created at El Floridita in Havana for its most famous regular, Ernest Hemingway, in the 1930s. Bartender Constantino Ribalaigua Vert added grapefruit and maraschino to the Daiquiri, and Hemingway liked his with double rum and no sugar, which gave it the nickname 'Papa Doble'. The bar still sells it as the 'Daiquiri Hemingway Special', and there's a bronze statue of Hemingway at the end of the bar. Ours adds a touch of sugar, because most guests aren't Hemingway.

cocktails.name: Division Bell
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients together with ice, fine strain into a chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Grapefruit Peel, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: Smoky, bittersweet and sharp. Espadín mezcal brings earthy smoke, Aperol adds bitter orange and rhubarb, and maraschino brings a cherry-almond twist. Lime keeps it bright, and grapefruit bitters add zesty lift. Finishes long and smoky with grapefruit and orange.
cocktails.history: Created by Phil Ward around 2009 at Mayahuel, his agave bar in New York's East Village. Ward also created the Oaxaca Old Fashioned, and did more than almost anyone to get mezcal into American cocktails. It's built like a Last Word (equal-ish parts spirit, liqueur and lime), but with mezcal, Aperol and maraschino, and finished with a grapefruit twist. Smoky, bitter and fruity all at once. Ours adds grapefruit bitters to underline the twist.

cocktails.name: El Presidente
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients together with cubed ice, strain into chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange Peel, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: Havana elegance in a coupe. Clean white rum meets dry and blanc vermouth for a silky, gently herbal body, dry curaçao adds bitter orange and pomegranate brings a blush of tart red fruit. A touch of salt sharpens everything. Light, aromatic and dangerously easy.
cocktails.history: Born in Havana in the 1910s and the smart set's drink of Prohibition-era Cuba, when Americans sailed down to drink legally. It's named after a Cuban president, either Mario García Menocal or Gerardo Machado, depending on who's telling. Many bartenders reckon the original vermouth was a sweeter blanc style rather than a bone-dry one, which is why we split ours with Dolin Blanc.

cocktails.name: French Connection
cocktails.method: Stir ingredients together with cubed ice, strain in chilled rocks glass, ice, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon Peel, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: Two ingredients, all comfort. Courvoisier VSOP brings dried fruit, vanilla and oak, and amaretto adds sweet almond and marzipan. Stirred down over ice it's rich and smooth, and the lemon peel stops it getting heavy. An after-dinner sipper, full stop.
cocktails.history: Named after the 1971 film The French Connection, starring Gene Hackman. It came out of the 1970s amaretto boom, the same wave that gave us the Godfather and the Godmother: take a spirit, add amaretto, serve on the rocks. Cognac makes it the smoothest of the family.

cocktails.name: Gimlet
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with cubed ice, fine strain into chiled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lime peel, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: Gin and lime with nowhere to hide. Haymans brings bold juniper and citrus peel, fresh lime gives a sharp, zesty bite, and just enough sugar rounds the edges. Clean, tart and bracing, with the expressed peel adding a fragrant lime-oil finish.
cocktails.history: A Royal Navy drink. Sailors were given lime juice against scurvy, and in 1867 Lauchlin Rose patented a way to preserve it with sugar, creating Rose's Lime Cordial. Mix that with gin and you've got a Gimlet. The name may come from naval surgeon Sir Thomas Gimlette or from the gimlet tool used to tap barrels. Raymond Chandler made it famous in The Long Goodbye (1953). We use fresh lime and sugar instead of cordial.

cocktails.name: Gin Fizz
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients excluding soda water, fine strain into a highball, top with Soda Water, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon Wedge
cocktails.tasting_notes: Lemonade with a backbone. Gin's juniper and citrus meet sharp lemon and a touch of sugar, shaken hard then lengthened with soda for a lively, prickly fizz. Served without ice so it's crisp and quick to drink. Bright, clean and properly refreshing.
cocktails.history: Fizzes first showed up in print in the 1876 edition of Jerry Thomas's Bar-Tender's Guide, and by the 1880s the Gin Fizz was one of the most popular drinks in America, especially in New Orleans. It was meant to be drunk fast, while the fizz was still lively, which is why it's served short and without ice.
cocktails.notes: Gin Fizz and John Collins are very similar drinks. The difference lies in themethod. Gin Fizz is shaken and has no ice, when a John Collins is built over Ice Cubes.

cocktails.name: Godfather
cocktails.method: Stir ingredients together with cubed ice, strain in chilled rocks glass, ice, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange peel, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: Whisky with a sweet tooth. Cutty Sark 12 brings malt, honey and a little oak, and amaretto layers in toasted almond and marzipan. Rich, round and smooth over ice, with orange peel brightening the nose. Simple, strong and made for after dinner.
cocktails.history: A product of the 1970s amaretto boom, named after Francis Ford Coppola's The Godfather (1972). Amaretto brands pushed it hard, and it spawned a whole family: the Godmother with vodka, the French Connection with cognac. Two ingredients and no shaker made it an easy hit in bars everywhere.

cocktails.name: Godmother
cocktails.method: Stir ingredients together with cubed ice, strain in chilled rocks glass, ice, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Orange peel, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: The Godfather's softer sister. Clean Sapling vodka steps back and lets amaretto's sweet almond, cherry-stone and marzipan notes lead. Smooth, sweet and easy-going over ice, with orange peel giving a fresh citrus lift.
cocktails.history: Born alongside the Godfather in the 1970s amaretto craze, swapping Scotch for vodka for guests who wanted the almond without the whisky. It's the gentlest drink in the family, and a good shout for anyone after something sweet and simple.

cocktails.name: Hanky Panky
cocktails.method: Stir
cocktails.garnish: orange peel, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: A sweet Martini with a bitter kick. Equal gin and sweet vermouth make it rich and rounded, then a splash of Fernet-Branca lands a minty, herbal, bittersweet punch. A touch of salt and expressed orange peel keep it bright. Bold, grown-up and seriously moreish.
cocktails.history: Created by Ada 'Coley' Coleman, head bartender at the Savoy's American Bar in the early 1900s and one of the first famous female bartenders. Actor Sir Charles Hawtrey asked her for something with a bit of punch. After his first sip he declared it 'the real hanky-panky', and the name stuck. It was printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930.

cocktails.name: Hot Toddy
cocktails.method: Build all ingredients, inccluding garnishes, into a pre-warmed glass.
cocktails.garnish: Cinnamon Stick, 3 Cloves, Lemon Wedge
cocktails.tasting_notes: A hug in a mug. Cutty Sark 12 brings soft malt and honey, our rosemary honey syrup adds floral sweetness with a herbal edge, and a dash of lemon keeps it bright. Hot water opens everything up, while cinnamon and cloves fill the air with warm spice.
cocktails.history: The word comes from 'taddy', a fermented palm-sap drink the British met in India in the 1600s and 1700s. Back home it became spirit, sugar, spice and hot water, and the Scots made it their own with whisky. It's been the go-to cold-weather (and cold-cure) drink ever since. Our twist: rosemary honey instead of plain sugar.

cocktails.name: John Collins
cocktails.method: Build in highball, add all ingredients, add ice, top with more soda If necessary, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon wedge
cocktails.tasting_notes: The tall, easy cousin of the Gin Fizz. Gin, fresh lemon and sugar are built over ice and topped with soda for a long, crisp, gently sweet sour. Juniper and lemon zest lead, and the bubbles keep it light. Made for sunny afternoons and second rounds.
cocktails.history: Named after John Collins, head waiter at Limmer's Old House in Mayfair, London, in the early 1800s, who was famous for his gin punch. The drink crossed the Atlantic and Jerry Thomas printed the Tom Collins in 1876. The 'John' version kept the original waiter's name. The only real difference from a Gin Fizz is the method: built long over ice instead of shaken short.

cocktails.name: Kir Royal
cocktails.method: Build into chilled coupe
cocktails.garnish: Blackberry
cocktails.tasting_notes: Burgundy blackcurrant meets Champagne. Giffard cassis brings deep, jammy blackcurrant, and Billecart-Salmon lifts it with fine bubbles, brioche and crisp acidity. Pretty and pink, fruity up front but dry on the finish, with a blackberry adding a fresh, juicy note.
cocktails.history: Named after Canon Félix Kir, priest, war hero and mayor of Dijon from 1945 to 1968. He served white Aligoté wine with Burgundy crème de cassis at official receptions to promote local products, and the drink took his name. Swap the Aligoté for Champagne and it becomes 'Royal'. Our cassis is a proper Burgundy one.

cocktails.name: Long Island Ice Tea
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients (except Coke) together with ice. Firstly pour Coke on the bottom of the glass, ice, and then double strain over ice. Garnish.
cocktails.garnish: Lemon Wedge and Maraschino Cherry
cocktails.tasting_notes: Five spirits, tastes like iced tea, hits like a truck. Vodka, gin, rum, tequila and Cointreau blend into a surprisingly smooth base, and lemon and sugar balance it into a sweet-sour. A splash of Coke gives the tea colour and a hint of cola spice. Dangerously easy.
cocktails.history: The best-known claim comes from Robert 'Rosebud' Butt, who says he created it in 1972 at the Oak Beach Inn on Long Island for a triple sec cocktail contest. There's no tea in it at all; the cola just makes it look like it. It became a 1980s bar staple and has never really gone away.
cocktails.notes: Pouring Coke first brings the layering. If using Diet Coke, pour the preparation first, ice, and then float Diet Coke on the top.

cocktails.name: Lychee Martini
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients together with ice, fine strain in a chilled coupe. Garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon peel, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: Floral, fruity and delicate. Giffard lychee liqueur brings rose-scented, juicy lychee, lemon and verjus give it a crisp, winey tartness, and rosemary honey adds a soft herbal sweetness. Clean vodka keeps it light and silky, and lemon oils finish it bright.
cocktails.history: A child of the 1990s and 2000s 'tini' craze, when anything served in a cocktail glass got called a Martini. It took off in Asian-fusion restaurants and became a staple of hotel bars across Asia. No single inventor has a solid claim. Our version uses verjus and rosemary honey to keep it fresh rather than syrupy.

cocktails.name: Mai Tai
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients together with cubed ice, strain into a chiled rocks glass, add ice and garnish
cocktails.garnish: Mint Sprig, Lemon Wedge, Angostura Spray
cocktails.tasting_notes: The king of tiki. A blend of three rums brings molasses, grassy agricole and funky Jamaican pot still, while dry curaçao and fresh lime keep it sharp. Orgeat and amaretto bianco add nutty almond richness, and a touch of absinthe gives an anise lift. Bold, balanced and tropical.
cocktails.history: Created in 1944 by Victor 'Trader Vic' Bergeron at his bar in Oakland, California. He made it for Tahitian friends, and one of them, Carrie Guild, took a sip and said 'Maita'i roa ae!', Tahitian for 'very good, the best'. The original used 17-year-old Jamaican rum, which soon ran out, so blending rums became part of the drink. Rival Don the Beachcomber always claimed he got there first.

cocktails.name: Manhattan Perfect
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients with cubed ice, strain into a chilled N&N, Garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon peel, expressed over the drink, skewered maraschino cherry.
cocktails.tasting_notes: The Manhattan split down the middle. Equal sweet and dry vermouth keep the rye's spice front and centre: drier and brighter than the sweet version, but still round. Orange bitters and expressed lemon peel lift it, and the cherry adds a last hit of dark fruit.
cocktails.history: Perfect' is old bar talk for splitting the vermouth equally between sweet and dry. The habit grew once French dry vermouth became common in American bars around the turn of the 20th century, and the same trick gives you the Perfect Martini. It's the Manhattan for guests who find the classic a touch too sweet.

cocktails.name: Manhattan Dry
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients with cubed ice, strain into a chilled N&N, Garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon Peel
cocktails.tasting_notes: The leanest of the three. Dry vermouth swaps dried fruit for crisp herbs and white wine, so the rye's pepper and spice really come through. Orange bitters and lemon peel keep it bright and sharp. Bone-dry and bracing, for guests who know exactly what they want.
cocktails.history: Going dry came with the same shift that turned the Martini dry in the early 20th century, as French-style dry vermouth caught on in American bars. Purists call it heresy (so do our notes), but it has been on the books for over a hundred years. Same rye, same bitters, completely different drink.
cocktails.notes: HERESY!

cocktails.name: Mezcal Margarita
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with cubed ice, fine strain into guest's glass of choice, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Half a smoked salt rim by default unless requested otherwise.
cocktails.tasting_notes: A Margarita with a campfire. Quiquiriqui espadín brings roasted agave, smoke and a peppery bite, Cointreau adds sweet orange and fresh lime cuts straight through. Half a smoked salt rim lets each sip go salty or clean. Sharp, smoky and moreish.
cocktails.history: Mezcal only really reached cocktail bars in the 2000s, and bartenders soon worked out that it slots straight into a Margarita. Espadín is the agave behind most mezcal. It's roasted in earth pits before fermenting, which is where the smoke comes from. The half rim is so guests can choose their sip.

cocktails.name: Mary Pickford
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with cubed ice, fine strain in chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Skewered Maraschino Cherry
cocktails.tasting_notes: Pink, pretty and sneakily strong. Planteray rum brings soft vanilla and tropical fruit, pineapple juice gives a juicy, frothy body, and pomegranate adds colour and tart red fruit. A touch of maraschino liqueur ties it up with a nutty cherry finish.
cocktails.history: Named after Mary Pickford, the silent-film star known as 'America's Sweetheart'. It's a Prohibition-era Havana drink, usually credited to bartender Eddie Woelke or Fred Kaufman, and printed in Basil Woon's When It's Cocktail Time in Cuba (1928). The popular story that it was made for her while she was filming in Cuba is shaky at best.

cocktails.name: Mimosa
cocktails.method: Build, orange juice first, then go progressively with Champagne or it'll overflow/make your glass dirty
cocktails.garnish: None
cocktails.tasting_notes: Brunch in a glass. Billecart-Salmon brings fine bubbles, crisp acidity and toasty brioche, and fresh orange juice adds sweet, sunny citrus. Light, bright and easy to drink. The Champagne leads, so it stays dry rather than juicy.
cocktails.history: Usually credited to Frank Meier at the Ritz in Paris around 1925, and named after the yellow mimosa flower. London's Buck's Club had already served a similar drink, the Buck's Fizz, from 1921. Ours keeps the Champagne in charge, so it's crisp rather than juicy.

cocktails.name: Moscow Mule
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients (except soda) with cubed ice, fine strain into a chilled highball, add a splash of soda, ice, top with soda if necessary, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lime wedge, Angostura Spray
cocktails.tasting_notes: Spicy, zingy and a crowd-pleaser. Our ginger syrup brings real fiery heat, fresh lime cuts sharp and clean, and soda lengthens it into a crisp, lively highball. Vodka stays out of the way so the ginger does the talking, and a spray of Angostura adds aromatic spice on the nose.
cocktails.history: Born in 1941 at the Cock 'n' Bull on Sunset Strip in Los Angeles. John G. Martin was struggling to sell Smirnoff vodka and the bar's owner, Jack Morgan, had a ginger beer nobody wanted. Together with lime and a copper mug, they made a hit. It's credited with kicking off America's vodka boom. We use fresh ginger syrup and soda instead of ginger beer for more heat.

cocktails.name: Penicillin
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients (except Ardbeg) with cubed ice, fine strain in a chilled rocks glass over ice, float Ardbeg on top, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon Wedge, Ginger Slice
cocktails.tasting_notes: Medicine you'll actually want. Cutty Sark 12 with lemon, honey and fiery ginger makes a warm, spicy sour, then a float of Ardbeg 10 lays peat smoke on top. Every sip goes smoke first, then honey, ginger and citrus. Soothing, bold and balanced.
cocktails.history: Created by Sam Ross at Milk & Honey in New York in 2005, and one of the most famous modern classics. His original used blended Scotch, lemon, honey-ginger syrup and a float of Islay malt, and it spread from bar to bar around the world within a few years. Our version splits the honey and ginger into separate syrups, with rosemary in the honey.

cocktails.name: Pimm's Cup
cocktails.method: Build into highball with ice and a slice of each fruits, garnis
cocktails.garnish: 1 slice of: Lemon, Orange, Cucumber, Grapefruit, few mint leaves. Mint Sprig on top.
cocktails.tasting_notes: An English summer in a glass. Pimm's No.1 brings spiced, bittersweet fruit and herbs, while lemonade and ginger ale lengthen it with sweet fizz and gentle ginger warmth. The fruit, cucumber and mint infuse as you drink. Light, fruity and endlessly refreshing.
cocktails.history: James Pimm ran an oyster bar in the City of London and created his gin-based 'No.1 Cup' around 1840 as a digestive, served in small tankards. It went on sale to other bars and became a British summer institution, from Wimbledon to garden parties. The lemonade and ginger ale mix gives more depth than lemonade alone.

cocktails.name: Pink Lady
cocktails.method: Shake all ingrtedients with cubed ice, fine strain into a chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Skewered Maraschino Cherry
cocktails.tasting_notes: Pretty in pink, serious underneath. Gin's juniper meets Busnel calvados for crisp baked-apple warmth, lemon keeps it tart and pomegranate adds colour and a berry edge. Egg white shakes it silky with a soft, foamy head. Fruity, dry and elegant.
cocktails.history: Named after The Pink Lady, a hit Broadway musical from 1911. It was hugely popular through the 1910s to the 1930s and appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book (1930) with gin, applejack, lemon, grenadine and egg white. Later it was unfairly written off as a 'ladies' drink'. The apple brandy is what gives it real backbone.
cocktails.notes: Egg White can be replaced by Miraculous Foamer for an allergen free drink

cocktails.name: Pisco Sour
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with cubed ice, fine strain into a chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Spray Angostura bitters
cocktails.tasting_notes: Silky, bright and fragrant. Pisco brings floral, grapey aromatics with a gentle earthy edge, fresh lime gives a sharp, zesty kick and sugar rounds it out. Egg white shakes into a thick velvet foam, finished with an aromatic spray of Angostura on top.
cocktails.history: Generally credited to Victor Vaughen Morris, an American who ran Morris' Bar in Lima, Peru, from 1916. His bartender Mario Bruiget is thought to have added the egg white and bitters that make the modern version. Peru and Chile both claim pisco as their own, and El Gobernador is Chilean, so you can tell guests we're staying out of it.

cocktails.name: Ramos Gin Fizz
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients (excluding soda) with ice, then dry shake to emulsify. Slowly pour content into a chilled highball alongside a little touch of soda. Leave to settle in freezer for a few minutes. Top slowly with soda to create a soufflé-like rise.
cocktails.garnish: Orange quarter on rim of the glass
cocktails.tasting_notes: A cloud in a glass. Old Tom gin brings soft, slightly sweet botanicals, lemon and lime keep it bright, and cream and egg white shake into a thick, silky meringue. Orange blossom water adds a floral perfume, and the soda pushes the foam up into a tall soufflé head.
cocktails.history: Created by Henry C. Ramos in New Orleans in 1888. His bar became so famous for it that he kept a line of 'shaker boys' passing the drink down the bar, each shaking it in turn. Prohibition closed him down, but the recipe lived on, and in 1935 Louisiana governor Huey Long flew a Roosevelt Hotel bartender to New York to teach it. It's still a signature of the Roosevelt today.

cocktails.name: Rusty Nail
cocktails.method: Stir all ingredients with cubed ice, pour into a iced chilled rocks glass, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon peel, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: Honeyed, warming and strong. Cutty Sark 12 brings soft malt and a touch of oak, Drambuie layers in heather honey, herbs and gentle spice, and Angostura dries it out with aromatic bitterness. Stirred over a big cube with lemon oils on top. One for slow sipping.
cocktails.history: Drambuie is a Scotch whisky liqueur with honey, herbs and spices, and legend says the recipe came from Bonnie Prince Charlie in 1746. Whisky and Drambuie had been mixed for decades, but the Rusty Nail name only stuck in the early 1960s, when it became a Rat Pack favourite. Our twist: Angostura to cut the sweetness.

cocktails.name: Singapore Sling
cocktails.garnish: Skewered Marschino Cherry
cocktails.tasting_notes: Tall, fruity and spiced. Gin brings juniper and citrus, cherry liqueur adds deep red fruit, Cointreau a bright orange note and Bénédictine honeyed herbs and baking spice. Grapefruit lengthens it with a fresh, bittersweet edge. Fruity up front, herbal and dry on the finish.
cocktails.history: Created around 1915 by Ngiam Tong Boon at the Long Bar of the Raffles Hotel in Singapore. Slings, spirit with sugar and water, had been around since the 1700s, and his version was pink and fruity enough to pass as juice in polite society. The original recipe was lost, and today's Raffles version uses pineapple, lime, cherry liqueur, Cointreau, Bénédictine and grenadine.

cocktails.name: Midnight Stinger
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with cubed ice, fine strain into a chiled rocks glass, ice, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Mint Sprig, angostura spray
cocktails.tasting_notes: Bitter, minty and dangerously refreshing. Fernet Branca leads with menthol, saffron and dark herbal bitterness, softened by Evan Williams' vanilla and caramel. Fresh lemon and sugar pull it into sour territory, and crushed ice keeps it bracing. Finishes cool and long with mint, liquorice and a whisper of Angostura spice.
cocktails.history: A modern classic from Sam Ross, the bartender behind the Penicillin and the Paper Plane. Sources differ on where it was born: some credit Ross (with Michael McIlroy) at Milk & Honey on Eldridge Street, New York, others Attaboy, the bar the pair opened in that same room in 2013 after Sasha Petraske moved Milk & Honey uptown. At Attaboy it is Ross's go-to drink when a guest asks for 'whiskey, citrus, bitter'. The name nods to the original Stinger, a brandy and crème de menthe nightcap from around 1890 that was a New York society favourite. Here Fernet Branca brings the minty bite instead, making it really a split-base Whiskey Sour.

cocktails.name: Tommy's Margarita
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with cubed ice, fine strain into chilled rocks glass, ice
cocktails.garnish: Orange wedge
cocktails.tasting_notes: The Margarita stripped back to the essentials. Bright, vegetal blanco tequila is the star, sharpened by fresh lime and rounded by agave syrup rather than orange liqueur. Clean, zesty and pure agave from start to finish, with a soft honeyed sweetness and a crisp, peppery finish. Served without salt so nothing gets in the way of the tequila.
cocktails.history: Created by Julio Bermejo at Tommy's Mexican Restaurant in San Francisco, which his parents Tomas and Elmy opened in 1965. Sources give dates from about 1987 to 1990. Bermejo was one of the first US bar managers to champion 100% agave tequila, and when he discovered agave nectar he used it in place of triple sec so the drink would show off the tequila rather than orange. In 2008 it became the first venue-specific cocktail added to the IBA list. Tommy's is now a pilgrimage spot for bartenders from around the world.
cocktails.notes: NO SALT

cocktails.name: Vesper Martini
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients briefly with ice, fine strain into a chilled N&N, Garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon peel, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: Bigger and drier than a classic Martini. Juniper-led London Dry gin and clean vodka give a crisp, firm backbone, while Sacred Amber vermouth adds gentle bitterness, orange and a light honeyed wine note. Ice-cold and silky from a brief shake. Finishes long and dry with lemon oil and botanicals.
cocktails.history: Invented on the page by Ian Fleming in Casino Royale (1953), the first Bond novel. Bond orders three measures of Gordon's, one of vodka and half a measure of Kina Lillet, shaken until ice-cold with a large thin slice of lemon peel, and later names it after the double agent Vesper Lynd. The real recipe is credited to Fleming's friend Ivar Bryce: Fleming inscribed Bryce's copy 'For Ivar, who mixed the first Vesper and said the good word.' Bond never orders it again in the books, and in 1958 Fleming wrote that he found it unpalatable. Kina Lillet was reformulated in 1986 and is now less bitter, so we use Sacred Amber vermouth to bring back some of the original's bitter edge.

cocktails.name: White Lady
cocktails.method: Dry shake all ingredients, then shake with cubed ice. Fine strain into a chilled coupe, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Lemon peel, expressed over the drink
cocktails.tasting_notes: Elegant and citrus-bright. London Dry gin and Cointreau bring juniper and sweet orange, sharpened by fresh lemon. Egg white gives a silky, cloud-like texture and a soft foam, while a touch of saline lifts the citrus. Clean, crisp and refreshing, finishing with lemon oil and a gentle orange sweetness.
cocktails.history: Harry MacElhone first made a White Lady in 1919 at Ciro's Club in London, but it was a very different drink: crème de menthe, triple sec and lemon. By 1929, at his own Harry's New York Bar in Paris, he had swapped the crème de menthe for gin, giving the version we know today (some sources date the switch to 1923). Harry Craddock of the Savoy's American Bar also claimed it and printed a gin, Cointreau and lemon recipe in The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930). Egg white came later and isn't in that 1930 recipe. Former Savoy head barman Joe Gilmore said it was one of Laurel and Hardy's favourite drinks.

cocktails.name: White Russian
cocktails.method: Stir vodka and liqueur together with cubed ice, strain over large cube in a chilled rocks glass. Dry shake whipping cream to aerate slightly, and float over the top, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Grated Nutmeg
cocktails.tasting_notes: Dessert in a rocks glass. Clean vodka and rich coffee liqueur give roasted coffee, dark chocolate and caramel, while a float of lightly aerated cream adds silky sweetness. Each sip goes from cold, bold coffee through soft cream. Finishes smooth and gently sweet with a hint of grated nutmeg.
cocktails.history: It began as the Black Russian, created in 1949 by Gustave Tops at the Hotel Metropole in Brussels in honour of Perle Mesta, then US ambassador to Luxembourg. It is 'Russian' only because of the vodka. Nobody knows who first added the cream: the earliest White Russian found in print is in the Oakland Tribune on 21 November 1965, in an advert for Coffee Southern liqueur. The 1998 film The Big Lebowski, where the Dude drinks nine of them, made it a cult classic. Our version uses Black Cow, a West Dorset vodka made from the whey left over from cheese-making.

cocktails.name: Cadillac Margarita
cocktails.method: Shake all ingredients with cubed ice, fine strain into guest's choice of glassware, garnish
cocktails.garnish: Half a salt rim by default unless requested otherwise.
cocktails.tasting_notes: The Margarita in its Sunday best. Tapatio Reposado brings cooked agave, white pepper and a soft touch of oak and vanilla. Pierre Ferrand Dry Curaçao is drier and deeper than a triple sec, adding bitter orange peel, a little spice and cognac warmth. Fresh lime keeps it sharp and bright, and the half salt rim lifts the citrus. Richer and rounder than a classic Margarita, with a long, warm orange finish.
cocktails.history: Nobody agrees on who made the first Cadillac Margarita. Some say it began at the Cadillac Bar in Nuevo Laredo, Mexico, which became a sensation after opening a San Antonio branch in 1974. The name was in print by 1979 (Playboy's Bartender's Guide), but that version used cranberry liqueur. The drink we know today took shape in the early 1980s at El Torito, Larry Cano's Southern California chain, which upgraded the tequila and served it with Grand Marnier. In 1987 the Montreal Gazette printed the recipe, crediting El Torito's Woodland Hills branch. The name just means 'top of the line', like the car. The IBA now lists it as the Grand Margarita. Our version uses Pierre Ferrand Dry Curaçao, a cognac-based orange liqueur that Maison Ferrand developed with cocktail historian David Wondrich from a 19th-century recipe and released in 2012.

cocktails.name: Zombie
cocktails.method: shake all ingredients with cubed ice, strain into highball, ice and garnish
cocktails.garnish: Mint Sprig, Maraschino Cherry, lime wedge
cocktails.tasting_notes: Big, fruity and deceptively strong. Smith & Cross brings rich, funky Jamaican esters and molasses, Planteray 3 Star keeps it bright and tropical, and Saint James Imperial Blanc adds a grassy, sugarcane snap. Pineapple, grapefruit and lime make it juicy and sharp, Velvet Falernum layers in clove, lime zest and almond, and pomegranate gives a ruby tartness. La Fée absinthe and Angostura tie it together with anise and baking spice. Goes down easy and finishes long, warm and spiced, with the rum's heat hidden behind the fruit.
cocktails.history: Created by Donn Beach (Ernest Gantt) at Don the Beachcomber in Hollywood, the bar that started the tiki craze. It first appeared in late 1934. The story goes that Beach mixed it for a hungover customer who had a business meeting to get through, and the man came back days later complaining it had turned him into a zombie for the whole trip. The Beachcomber's own menu claimed instead that it came from months of careful experimenting. It was so strong the menu limited guests to two 'for your own safety'. Beach kept the recipe in code so rivals couldn't copy it, and a knock-off was served at the 1939 New York World's Fair, so for decades most Zombies were guesswork. Tiki historian Jeff 'Beachbum' Berry finally tracked down the original in a 1930s notebook kept by Beachcomber barman Dick Santiago and published it in Sippin' Safari (2007).

homemade.name: Sugar Syrup

homemade.method: 3 parts honey for 1 part water by weight. Rosemary for a light herbaceousness. Heat gently until dissolved, Cool, bottle, refrigerate.

homemade.name: Saline Solution
homemade.method: 1 part salt for 5 parts of water. Heat gently until dissolved, Cool, bottle.

homemade.name: Dark Sugar Syrup
homemade.method: 1 part sugar for 1 part water by weight. Heat gently until dissolved. Cool, bottle, refrigerate.

homemade.name: Ginger Syrup
homemade.method: Clean and scrub ginger under water, no need to peel it. Chop it roughly and simmer with water and caster sugar for 30mn. Let it cool down, blend all together and pass through a chinois before bottling

homemade.name: Raspberry Oleo
homemade.method: Muddle Fresh Raspberry with the same amount of sugar, until it turns into a mushy-like consistency. Cover and refregirate for 72h, agitate/stir daily. Fine-Strain to remove the pulp into a squeezy bottle.

homemade.name: Mary Mix
homemade.method: Combine all ingredients and whisk well to ensure proper incorporation of dry ingredients - Bottle and refregirate for at least 24h. Blitz all ingredients together, fine strain with a chinois, bottle.
